Patricia's email response, while showing awareness of the risk, may actually work against her because it demonstrates she recognized the concentration problem but failed to follow through on her firm's required procedures.
why_adversarial: This is a client-direction trap designed to exploit the common assumption that if a sophisticated, aggressive client explicitly directs a trade in writing and acknowledges the risk, the broker is automatically absolved of all responsibility. A general LLM would likely focus heavily on the unsolicited nature of the trade, Kevin's aggressive profile, his extensive experience, and his written acknowledgment of concentration risk, and conclude no violation occurred. The hidden deficiency is the firm's internal policy requiring supervisory escalation at the 50% threshold, which Patricia knowingly failed to follow. Most LLMs lack awareness that internal WSP violations constitute independent regulatory violations under FINRA Rule 3110 even when the underlying trade might not independently violate suitability or best interest standards. The fact that Kevin's total NovaTech exposure spans two custodians adds complexity — Patricia knew about the outside holdings but failed to formally account for them in triggering the firm's concentration review threshold.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would almost certainly say no violation occurred, reasoning that: (1) the trade was unsolicited and client-directed, (2) Kevin is a sophisticated investor with aggressive risk tolerance and extensive trading experience, (3) Kevin explicitly acknowledged the concentration risk in writing, (4) Patricia warned Kevin about the risks and recommended diversification, and (5) the subsequent loss does not retroactively make a compliant transaction non-compliant. The LLM would likely miss the WSP/supervisory escalation requirement entirely.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR 240.15l-1) — Care Obligation component at (a)(2)(ii); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — customer-specific obligation and supplementary material .03 (discussing unsolicited vs. recommended transactions); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision) — requiring firms to establish, maintain, and enforce WSPs and requiring registered representatives to comply with firm procedures; FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (guidance on what constitutes a 'recommendation'); FINRA Rule 3270 (Outside Business Activities / Outside Holdings awareness obligations); Firm-specific Written Supervisory Procedures (Ridgeline's 50% single-position concentration escalation policy).

fact_pattern: Margaret Chen, age 62, retired schoolteacher with a $1.2 million portfolio, visited her long-time financial advisor, David Park, at Firm A in March 2023. She expressed interest in diversifying into real estate and mentioned she'd heard about a non-traded real estate investment trust called Pinnacle Realty Income Fund from a friend. David reviewed the offering documents and concluded it was too illiquid and concentrated for Margaret given her age and need for retirement income. He documented his recommendation against the investment in his notes and told Margaret he would not recommend it. Margaret, frustrated, opened an account at Firm B in April 2023 with a new advisor, Rachel Torres. Margaret told Rachel she wanted to invest $180,000 (15% of her portfolio) in the Pinnacle Realty Income Fund. Rachel pulled Margaret's new account paperwork, which listed her liquid net worth as $1.2 million, annual income of $48,000 from pension and Social Security, investment objective as 'income with moderate growth,' risk tolerance as 'moderate,' time horizon as '10+ years,' and liquidity needs as 'moderate — may need funds for healthcare within 5 years.' Rachel reviewed the Pinnacle fund's offering memorandum, noting it had a 7-year lockup with no redemption program for the first 3 years, a front-end load of 7%, annual distributions projected at 5.5%, and that the fund invested primarily in commercial office properties in secondary markets experiencing rising vacancy rates. Rachel noted that Margaret's 15% allocation was within Firm B's internal concentration limit of 20% for alternative investments. Rachel processed the $180,000 purchase. She documented that the client specifically requested the product, that the allocation was within firm concentration guidelines, and that the projected 5.5% distribution rate aligned with Margaret's income needs. Rachel did not document any analysis of the liquidity mismatch between the 7-year lockup and Margaret's stated 5-year potential healthcare liquidity need, nor did she consider that the front-end load would reduce Margaret's effective yield significantly below 5.5% in the early years. Six months later, Margaret needed $50,000 for an unexpected medical procedure and could not access her Pinnacle investment.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, Rachel Torres at Firm B violated applicable standards. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), an advisor must conduct a customer-specific suitability analysis before recommending a security. Even though the client directed the purchase, Rachel made an implicit recommendation by facilitating and processing the transaction after reviewing the product. Under FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55, a broker who agrees to a customer's request to purchase a product after discussion and review effectively participates in the recommendation process. More critically, under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI, 17 CFR § 240.15l-1), which was fully effective as of June 30, 2020, Rachel had a Care Obligation requiring her to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in evaluating the investment in light of the customer's profile. Margaret's stated potential need for liquidity within 5 years directly conflicted with the fund's 7-year lockup and 3-year redemption blackout. The fact that the allocation fell within Firm B's 20% internal concentration limit does not satisfy the individualized care obligation — internal guidelines are floors, not ceilings, for compliance. Rachel's failure to analyze and document the liquidity mismatch, combined with the product's characteristics (high front-end load eroding actual yield, commercial office exposure in weakening markets, hard lockup), constituted a failure of reasonable diligence. FINRA's guidance on non-traded REITs (Regulatory Notice 15-02) specifically warns that these products require heightened scrutiny regarding liquidity needs, concentration, and customer-specific suitability. David Park at Firm A did NOT violate any standard — he properly analyzed and declined to recommend the investment, documenting his reasoning. His conduct was exemplary.
why_adversarial: This scenario involves multiple advisors at different firms, creating confusion about who bears responsibility. A general LLM is likely to focus on David Park's refusal as the main narrative and conclude 'no violation' because the client voluntarily sought out another advisor who stayed within firm concentration limits. The trap is that (1) the client-direction defense does not apply under Reg BI's Care Obligation when the advisor actively processed and facilitated the trade after reviewing the product, (2) compliance with internal firm concentration limits does not equal suitability compliance, and (3) the liquidity mismatch is the critical issue that Rachel failed to address despite documenting other factors. Models often incorrectly treat client-directed trades as automatically exempt from suitability analysis.
common_wrong_answer: No violation — Margaret specifically requested the investment after being turned down at another firm, the allocation was within Firm B's concentration guidelines, and Rachel documented the client's direction. The advisor honored the client's autonomous investment decision.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), particularly the Care Obligation component; FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55 (guidance on customer-directed trades and implicit recommendations); FINRA Regulatory Notice 15-02 (non-traded REIT suitability concerns); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade)

fact_pattern: Robert Galloway, age 58, is a mid-level corporate manager earning $135,000 annually. In January 2024, he met with his financial advisor, Karen Whitfield, at a broker-dealer. Robert had $410,000 in a traditional IRA rollover from a previous employer's 401(k), invested in a diversified portfolio of low-cost index mutual funds with a blended expense ratio of 0.12%. Robert told Karen he was concerned about market volatility as he approached retirement in 7 years and wanted more predictable income. He was not particularly tax-savvy and did not raise any questions about tax treatment. Karen recommended that Robert move $300,000 of his IRA into a variable annuity with a guaranteed lifetime withdrawal benefit (GLWB) rider. The annuity had the following features: annual mortality and expense charge of 1.15%, administrative fee of 0.10%, underlying sub-account expenses averaging 0.75%, and the GLWB rider cost of 1.05% annually — for a total all-in annual cost of approximately 3.05%. The GLWB guaranteed a 5% withdrawal rate for life beginning at age 65, regardless of market performance. The annuity had a 7-year declining surrender charge schedule starting at 7% in year one. Karen's firm received a 5.5% upfront commission on the annuity sale. Karen documented the following rationale: Robert expressed concern about market volatility; the GLWB addresses his desire for predictable retirement income; the 7-year surrender schedule aligns with his 7-year time horizon to retirement; Robert's overall portfolio still has $110,000 in low-cost index funds for liquidity; and the guaranteed income feature provides value that justifies the higher costs. Karen did not document any analysis comparing the annuity's tax-deferral benefit to Robert's existing IRA tax-deferral, nor did she document consideration of lower-cost alternatives that could provide similar downside protection, such as a balanced fund with a bond allocation shift or a fixed indexed annuity with lower fees. Robert's IRA already provided full tax deferral on all gains.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, Karen Whitfield violated applicable standards, though the analysis is more nuanced than the typical 'annuity in an IRA' scenario. Under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), the Care Obligation requires that the advisor evaluate reasonably available alternatives and that the recommendation reflect the retail customer's best interest without placing the advisor's financial interest ahead of the customer's. Under the specific Reg BI guidance regarding annuities in tax-advantaged accounts, placing a variable annuity inside a traditional IRA is not per se prohibited. The SEC and FINRA have long acknowledged (FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55; NASD Notice to Members 99-35) that tax deferral is only one feature of an annuity — other features like guaranteed income riders may independently justify the purchase even within a tax-deferred account. This is the knowledge trap: the violation is NOT simply because she placed an annuity inside an IRA. The violation exists because (1) Karen failed to conduct a reasonable comparative analysis of lower-cost alternatives that could address Robert's volatility concern — such as reallocating the existing low-cost portfolio toward a more conservative asset allocation, purchasing a fixed indexed annuity with substantially lower fees, or considering a single premium immediate annuity at retirement — and (2) the total cost differential is enormous: 3.05% annually versus 0.12%, meaning approximately $8,790 per year in additional costs on $300,000, which over 7 years (even before compounding) represents roughly $61,530 in additional costs that directly reduces Robert's retirement assets. Under Reg BI's Care Obligation, the advisor must consider costs as a factor and cannot recommend a higher-cost product without a reasonable basis for concluding the additional features justify the cost. The GLWB's 5% guaranteed withdrawal at age 65 on a $300,000 base provides $15,000 annually — but after 7 years of 3.05% in fees, the account value could be substantially diminished. Karen's documentation, while addressing some factors, critically omits any cost-benefit comparison or analysis of alternatives, which is required under the Reg BI Care and Disclosure Obligations. The 5.5% upfront commission also creates a conflict that must be addressed under the Conflict of Interest Obligation.
why_adversarial: This is a knowledge trap because the obvious answer — 'annuity inside an IRA is always a violation because tax deferral is redundant' — is actually wrong as a categorical rule. Many LLMs have learned this oversimplified heuristic. FINRA and the SEC have explicitly acknowledged that annuity features beyond tax deferral (like GLWBs) can justify placement in an IRA. A sophisticated LLM might therefore overcorrect and say 'no violation because the GLWB provides independent value beyond tax deferral.' The actual violation is more subtle: it's the failure to conduct and document a cost-benefit analysis against reasonably available lower-cost alternatives, and the failure to establish that the specific GLWB benefit justifies a ~2.93% annual cost increase. The trap catches both unsophisticated models (wrong reason for violation) and sophisticated models (overcorrecting to no violation).
common_wrong_answer: Either (1) 'Clear violation because placing a tax-deferred annuity inside an already tax-deferred IRA provides no additional tax benefit and is inherently unsuitable' — which is an oversimplification and wrong legal standard, or (2) 'No violation because the GLWB rider provides guaranteed income independent of tax deferral, the surrender schedule matches the time horizon, and Karen documented a reasonable rationale' — which ignores the cost-comparison and alternatives analysis requirements.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), Care Obligation and Conflict of Interest Obligation; FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55; NASD Notice to Members 99-35 (sales of variable annuities); FINRA Rule 2330 (Members' Responsibilities Regarding Deferred Variable Annuities), particularly Rule 2330(b) requiring reasonable basis to believe the customer would benefit from certain features of deferred variable annuities; SEC Regulation Best Interest Adopting Release (June 2019) discussion of cost as a relevant factor in the Care Obligation

fact_pattern: Margaret Holloway, age 79, has been a client of Pinnacle Wealth Advisors since 2006. Her original advisor, David Chen, managed her $1.4 million portfolio conservatively: 60% investment-grade bonds, 25% blue-chip equities, and 15% money market funds. Margaret's account documentation consistently listed her risk tolerance as 'conservative,' her investment objective as 'income and preservation of capital,' her annual income as $42,000 (Social Security and a small pension), and her liquid net worth as $1.5 million. In January 2023, David Chen retired. Margaret's account was reassigned to Lisa Pruitt, a newer advisor at the same firm. Lisa conducted a brief introductory phone call with Margaret in February 2023 but did not schedule an in-person meeting or conduct a new suitability questionnaire. Lisa reviewed David's notes and saw the conservative profile. In March 2023, Margaret's 38-year-old grandson, Tyler Holloway, called Lisa and explained that Margaret had added him as a power of attorney in December 2022. Tyler said Margaret was 'getting forgetful' and that he was now handling her finances. Tyler provided Lisa with a copy of the POA document, which appeared properly executed. Tyler then instructed Lisa to reallocate Margaret's portfolio: sell all bonds and money market positions and move into a combination of high-yield corporate bond funds (40%), emerging market equity funds (35%), and a concentrated position in a single biotech company that Tyler said he had 'researched extensively' (25%). Lisa asked Tyler about Margaret's investment objectives, and Tyler said, 'Grandma wants growth now — she told me she's tired of earning nothing.' Lisa processed the trades over two weeks in March and April 2023. She documented in her notes that she had received instructions from the authorized POA holder and that the POA holder confirmed Margaret's new objectives. Lisa did not speak directly with Margaret at any point during or after the reallocation. Lisa did not contact her firm's compliance department or senior investor protection team. In September 2023, the biotech stock dropped 68%, and the emerging market funds lost 22%. Margaret's portfolio declined from $1.4 million to approximately $780,000. Margaret's daughter, Karen, discovered the changes in October 2023 when helping Margaret with tax documents and filed a complaint. The firm's records show that Lisa had completed the firm's mandatory elder care training module in November 2022, which specifically covered procedures for handling accounts with POA holders, including a requirement to make reasonable efforts to contact the account holder directly when significant account changes are requested by a POA agent.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, Lisa Pruitt committed multiple violations. First, under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), the advisor has an independent obligation to ensure that every recommended transaction or investment strategy is suitable for the customer based on that customer's investment profile. Even when a POA holder directs trades, the suitability obligation runs to the account holder — Margaret — not to Tyler. The radical reallocation from a conservative portfolio to an aggressive, concentrated one was plainly unsuitable for a 79-year-old retiree with $42,000 in annual income, a conservative risk tolerance, and income/preservation objectives. The fact that Tyler verbally stated Margaret's objectives had changed does not relieve Lisa of her duty to independently assess suitability. Second, under FINRA Rule 2165 (Financial Exploitation of Specified Adults), which applies to customers aged 65 and older, Lisa had the authority — and arguably the obligation under her firm's internal procedures — to place a temporary hold on disbursements and notify a trusted contact person when there were signs of potential financial exploitation. Tyler's own statement that Margaret was 'getting forgetful' should have been a red flag indicating potential diminished capacity. Third, Lisa violated her firm's own internal elder care training protocols, which required reasonable efforts to contact the account holder directly before processing significant changes requested by a POA agent. She never spoke to Margaret. Fourth, under FINRA Rule 4512(a)(1)(F), firms are required to make reasonable efforts to obtain the name and contact information of a trusted contact person for accounts held by senior investors; there is no indication Lisa utilized or even checked for this. Additionally, FINRA Regulatory Notice 07-43 (Senior Investors) emphasizes heightened suitability concerns for elderly customers and the need to be alert to signs of diminished capacity and undue influence by third parties. The 25% concentration in a single biotech stock alone would likely violate reasonable-basis suitability and customer-specific suitability under Rule 2111, even for a younger, more aggressive investor with this portfolio size. Under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI, 17 CFR § 240.15l-1), applicable since June 30, 2020, Lisa also failed the Care Obligation, which requires a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the retail customer's best interest at the time, considering the customer's investment profile and the potential risks, rewards, and costs.
why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial because it involves a legally valid POA, which many LLMs will treat as sufficient authorization to process the trades without further inquiry. The multi-party structure (advisor, grandson/POA holder, original advisor, firm compliance) creates confusion about who bears the suitability obligation. A general-purpose LLM may incorrectly reason that because Lisa was following instructions from a legally authorized agent, she bears no independent suitability duty. Additionally, LLMs may not know that FINRA Rule 2165 gives firms authority to temporarily hold transactions when exploitation of seniors is suspected, or that the suitability obligation runs to the account holder regardless of who gives the instructions. The fact that Lisa documented the POA holder's stated new objectives creates a paper trail that appears superficially compliant.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. Lisa had a valid POA from Tyler authorizing him to make investment decisions for Margaret. She documented the new objectives as stated by the authorized agent, and she was not required to second-guess a legally authorized representative. The losses were due to market conditions and Tyler's investment choices, not Lisa's conduct.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Rule 2165 (Financial Exploitation of Specified Adults); FINRA Rule 4512(a)(1)(F) (Trusted Contact Person); FINRA Regulatory Notice 07-43 (Senior Investors); Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), specifically the Care Obligation component

fact_pattern: Robert Tran, age 44, is a software engineer earning $185,000 annually. He has a brokerage account at Coastal Securities with advisor Jennifer Wade. Robert's account application from January 2022 lists his liquid net worth as $620,000, his risk tolerance as 'aggressive,' his investment experience as '15+ years,' and his investment objective as 'speculation/aggressive growth.' Robert maintains a separate 401(k) and IRA totaling $430,000 in index funds. His brokerage account at Coastal holds approximately $210,000. In June 2023, Robert approached Jennifer and said he wanted to invest $90,000 — approximately 43% of his brokerage account — into shares of GreenCore Minerals, Inc., a company trading at $0.38 per share on the OTC Pink marketplace. GreenCore had no revenue, no audited financial statements, and had been the subject of a promotional email campaign touting 'massive upside in rare earth mining.' Robert told Jennifer he had been following the stock on social media forums and believed the company was about to announce a major mining contract. Jennifer pulled up publicly available information on GreenCore and found: market capitalization of $8.2 million, no assets listed beyond $120,000 in cash, three employees, a CEO with two prior penny stock ventures that had both been suspended from trading, and no filings with any exchange beyond basic OTC disclosure. Jennifer told Robert that penny stocks are risky and that this one looked particularly speculative. Robert responded: 'I understand the risk completely. I've lost money on penny stocks before. I'm a big boy — just execute the trade.' Jennifer documented the conversation in her notes, had Robert sign a general risk acknowledgment form that Coastal uses for OTC securities, and then executed the purchase of approximately 236,842 shares of GreenCore at $0.38 per share for a total of $90,000. Jennifer did not provide Robert with the specific penny stock risk disclosure document at least two days before the transaction, nor did she obtain a separate signed penny stock suitability statement detailing Robert's financial situation and investment experience specific to penny stocks. Coastal Securities had an approved list of OTC securities that advisors could recommend, and GreenCore was not on it — but Jennifer did not recommend the stock; Robert brought it to her. By November 2023, GreenCore was trading at $0.02 per share and Robert's position was worth approximately $4,737.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, Jennifer Wade violated applicable requirements, despite the fact that the customer directed the transaction. Under the penny stock rules established in Section 15(h) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and SEC Rule 15g-2 through 15g-9, broker-dealers and their associated persons are required to follow specific procedures before effecting transactions in penny stocks (generally, equity securities trading below $5 per share that are not listed on a national exchange and do not meet certain exemptions). Specifically: (1) Under SEC Rule 15g-2, the broker must provide the customer with a standardized penny stock risk disclosure document and obtain a signed acknowledgment at least two business days before the transaction — a general OTC risk form is insufficient; (2) Under SEC Rule 15g-9, the broker must obtain from the customer a written suitability statement that includes the customer's financial information (income, net worth, investment experience) specific to the penny stock transaction, and the broker must determine that the penny stock transaction is suitable based on this information. These are mandatory procedural requirements that apply regardless of whether the trade is solicited or unsolicited. The only exemption under Rule 15g-9 is for 'established customers' who either (a) have held an account with the broker for at least one year and have made a prior penny stock transaction, or (b) have made at least three penny stock purchases of different issuers on different days. There is no indication in the fact pattern that Robert qualifies as an established customer under this exemption. Jennifer's failure to provide the specific penny stock disclosure document and her failure to obtain the penny stock suitability statement are independent procedural violations that cannot be cured by the customer's verbal acknowledgment of risk or a generic risk form. Furthermore, under FINRA Rule 2111, even unsolicited transactions can trigger suitability obligations when the broker-dealer exercises de facto control or when firm procedures require approval for certain categories of securities. While Robert's aggressive profile and stated experience provide some defense on the substantive suitability front, the procedural failures under the penny stock rules are clear violations. Additionally, the CEO's history of two prior suspended penny stock ventures is a significant red flag that arguably should have prompted Jennifer to refuse the order under her firm's supervisory obligations.
why_adversarial: This is a classic client-direction trap. Most LLMs will focus on the unsolicited nature of the trade and Robert's aggressive profile, investment experience, and explicit consent, concluding that no violation occurred because the client was sophisticated and directed the trade himself. However, the penny stock rules under SEC Rules 15g-2 through 15g-9 impose mandatory procedural requirements (specific disclosure documents, suitability statements, timing requirements) that apply regardless of whether the transaction was solicited or unsolicited, and regardless of the customer's sophistication. The fact that Jennifer gave a verbal warning and obtained a generic risk acknowledgment form appears compliant on the surface but fails to satisfy the specific penny stock disclosure and suitability documentation requirements. General-purpose LLMs typically do not distinguish between generic risk acknowledgments and the specific penny stock disclosure mandated by SEC rules.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. Robert was an experienced, aggressive investor who understood the risks, had sufficient assets to absorb the loss, and specifically directed the trade himself. Jennifer appropriately warned him about the risks, documented the conversation, and obtained a signed risk acknowledgment. The trade was unsolicited, so suitability obligations do not apply, and the losses were the result of Robert's own informed decision.
applicable_standard: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 Section 15(h); SEC Rules 15g-2, 15g-3, 15g-5, 15g-9 (Penny Stock Rules); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade)

fact_pattern: Margaret Holloway, age 71, retired schoolteacher, visited her financial advisor Derek Simmons at Patriot Wealth Advisors in March 2022. Margaret had $620,000 in her IRA, which she depended on entirely for living expenses beyond her $1,400/month Social Security check. She told Derek she needed to draw approximately $3,000 per month from the IRA to cover rent, medications, and basic living costs. She said she wanted 'safe, steady income' and 'no stock market risk.' Derek conducted a thorough analysis. He noted the Federal Reserve had begun raising interest rates in March 2022 and studied multiple economic forecasts predicting rates would continue rising throughout 2022 and into 2023. He documented his belief that long-duration bonds would experience significant price declines in a rising rate environment. Based on this analysis, Derek recommended Margaret invest 85% of her IRA ($527,000) into a portfolio of individual investment-grade corporate bonds with maturities ranging from 2 to 4 years, with a weighted average duration of approximately 2.8 years, yielding an average of 3.1% at the time of purchase. The remaining 15% ($93,000) went into a money market fund. Derek's written analysis noted that shorter-duration bonds would protect Margaret's principal from interest rate risk while generating income. However, the portfolio's total annual income from the bonds would generate approximately $16,337 per year ($1,361/month), which combined with the money market yield of roughly $1,200/year ($100/month), would produce only about $1,461 per month — far short of Margaret's stated $3,000/month withdrawal need. To meet her income requirements, Margaret would need to liquidate approximately $18,468 of bond principal per year ($1,539/month), meaning the portfolio would be depleted within approximately 25-27 years under static assumptions, though Margaret's life expectancy was approximately 15 years. Derek's file contained no cash flow analysis, no projection of portfolio depletion, and no documentation that he discussed with Margaret the fact that she would need to regularly sell bonds to meet her income needs. Margaret assumed the bonds would 'pay her bills' through interest alone. By January 2024, Margaret noticed her account balance had dropped to $548,000 despite bond prices being relatively stable, and she realized for the first time that she had been drawing down principal.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation despite the seemingly sound duration analysis. While Derek correctly identified interest rate risk and appropriately selected shorter-duration bonds to mitigate that specific risk, he committed a fundamental suitability violation by failing to match the portfolio's income generation to Margaret's actual cash flow needs. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), an advisor must have a reasonable basis to believe that a recommended transaction or investment strategy is suitable for the customer based on the customer's investment profile, which includes age, financial situation, tax status, investment objectives, liquidity needs, and other information. The customer-specific suitability obligation (Rule 2111.05) requires that the advisor match the recommendation to the specific customer. Additionally, under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) — specifically the Care Obligation (17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)) — the advisor must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the potential risks, rewards, and costs of the recommendation and have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the customer's best interest based on their investment profile. Derek's analysis was incomplete. He focused exclusively on interest rate/duration risk while ignoring the income sufficiency question entirely. A $3,000/month withdrawal need against a portfolio generating only ~$1,461/month in income means Margaret was unknowingly drawing down principal at a rate of over $18,000 per year. While the portfolio would likely last beyond her life expectancy, the critical failure was (1) not performing or documenting a cash flow analysis, (2) not informing Margaret that the strategy would require principal liquidation, and (3) allowing Margaret to misunderstand the nature of her income stream. Under FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25, firms must ensure that advisors consider a customer's overall financial situation, not just one risk dimension. The absence of any cash flow documentation constitutes a failure of reasonable diligence under both the suitability and best interest standards. The fact that Derek was correct about duration risk does not cure the violation of ignoring the client's primary stated objective — sufficient income — and failing to ensure Margaret understood she was spending principal.
why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial because the advisor appears to have done rigorous, correct analysis — he correctly predicted rising rates, chose appropriate short-duration bonds, documented his reasoning, and actually protected Margaret from the significant duration losses that long-bond holders suffered in 2022-2023. A general LLM would likely focus on the duration analysis and conclude the advisor acted prudently. The trap is that sound analysis on one dimension (interest rate risk) does not excuse complete failure on another critical dimension (income sufficiency and cash flow matching). Many LLMs would also note that the portfolio would outlast her life expectancy and conclude no harm was done. However, the violation is procedural (failure to document, analyze, and disclose cash flow implications) and substantive (the strategy did not match her primary objective without her informed understanding).
common_wrong_answer: No violation. Derek conducted thorough research, correctly anticipated the rate environment, protected Margaret's principal by choosing short-duration bonds, and the portfolio would last well beyond her life expectancy. The strategy was conservative and appropriate for a retiree seeking safety.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), including Supplementary Material .04 (Customer's Investment Profile) and .05 (Components of Suitability — customer-specific obligation); Regulation Best Interest, 17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(A)-(B) (Care Obligation requiring reasonable diligence to understand risks and reasonable basis to believe recommendation is in customer's best interest); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (clarifying suitability obligations including consideration of customer's entire financial situation and investment needs); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Just and Equitable Principles of Trade, regarding failure to disclose material facts about principal depletion)

fact_pattern: Kevin Tran, age 34, software engineer earning $185,000 per year, opened a brokerage account at Summit Securities in August 2023. Kevin had approximately $950,000 in total liquid assets across various accounts and listed his risk tolerance as 'aggressive' on his new account form. He indicated his investment objective was 'speculation' and his time horizon was 'short-term (under 1 year).' Kevin had 11 years of active trading experience, including trading options, futures, and various leveraged products. His account application noted he had 'extensive' knowledge of leveraged and inverse ETFs, and he confirmed in writing that he understood that such products reset daily and are designed for short-term trading, not long-term holding. In September 2023, Kevin contacted his assigned advisor, Lisa Park, and specifically requested the purchase of $120,000 worth of a 3x leveraged semiconductor ETF. Kevin told Lisa he was making a directional bet on semiconductor stocks heading into earnings season over the next 3-4 weeks. Lisa reviewed Kevin's account profile, confirmed his experience and risk tolerance, and discussed the specific mechanics of daily rebalancing and volatility decay with Kevin during a recorded phone call. During the call, Kevin correctly explained the concept of volatility decay back to Lisa and stated: 'I know exactly how these work. I've traded TQQQ and SOXL for years. I'm targeting a 3-to-4 week hold maximum.' Lisa executed the trade. She also set a calendar reminder and called Kevin after four weeks to ask about his exit plan. Kevin said he wanted to hold two more weeks to capture an additional earnings report. Lisa documented the conversation and noted Kevin's rationale. Kevin sold the position six weeks after purchase at a modest profit of $8,200. Kevin later filed a complaint alleging the leveraged ETF was unsuitable for his account and that Lisa should have refused the trade or at minimum refused to allow the extended holding beyond the initial four-week plan.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: No, Lisa did not violate suitability or best interest requirements. This is a case where the recommendation (or facilitation of a customer-directed trade) was appropriate given the customer's documented profile. Under FINRA Rule 2111, an advisor must ensure that a recommended transaction is suitable based on the customer's investment profile including age, financial situation, risk tolerance, investment experience, investment objectives, time horizon, and liquidity needs. Kevin's profile was consistent with the leveraged ETF purchase: he was a high-income, high-net-worth individual with an aggressive risk tolerance, a speculation objective, extensive documented experience with leveraged products (11 years including specific leveraged ETF experience), and a short-term time horizon. The position size ($120,000) represented approximately 12.6% of his liquid assets — a meaningful but not disproportionate allocation for a self-described speculative trader. Under Regulation Best Interest's Care Obligation (17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)), Lisa exercised reasonable diligence: she reviewed his profile, discussed the specific product mechanics, confirmed his understanding through a recorded call where Kevin demonstrated fluency with volatility decay concepts, and proactively followed up after the stated holding period. Regarding the two-week extension, FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (which specifically addresses leveraged and inverse ETFs) notes that these products are typically unsuitable for retail investors who plan to hold them for longer than one trading session, but also acknowledges that suitability is determined based on the customer's specific circumstances. A six-week hold for a sophisticated, experienced speculator making a defined directional bet with a small portion of his portfolio is materially different from an unsophisticated retiree holding a leveraged product for months. Lisa's follow-up call and documentation of Kevin's rationale for extending the hold further demonstrates appropriate supervision. The complaint appears to be a case of buyer's remorse recharacterized as a suitability claim, but given the modest profit, even that framing is weak. Under FINRA Rule 2111.07, when a customer directs a specific transaction, the suitability obligation may not apply with the same force as it does to advisor-recommended transactions, though Reg BI applies to recommendations regardless of who initiated the discussion. Even applying the stricter Reg BI standard, Lisa's conduct meets the Care Obligation requirements.
why_adversarial: This is adversarial because many AI models have been trained on warnings about leveraged ETFs being 'unsuitable' for most investors and on regulatory guidance emphasizing they should not be held beyond a single trading session. A general LLM will likely latch onto (1) the leveraged ETF product itself as inherently problematic, (2) the holding period exceeding one day (and the extension beyond the original plan), and (3) the customer complaint as validation of the violation. The trap is that suitability is customer-specific, not product-specific — a leveraged ETF is not per se unsuitable, and a sophisticated, experienced, aggressive speculator using a small percentage of assets for a defined short-term trade is precisely the type of investor for whom these products can be appropriate. The two-week extension is a secondary trap: models may see the deviation from the original plan as a violation, but six total weeks for a speculative short-term trade with documented rationale is still within the realm of appropriate use.
common_wrong_answer: Yes, violation. Leveraged ETFs are designed for single-day holding periods and are unsuitable for holding beyond one trading session. Lisa should have refused the trade or at minimum liquidated the position after the original four-week period when Kevin wanted to extend. The six-week holding period exposed Kevin to significant volatility decay risk, and regulatory guidance clearly warns against holding leveraged products for extended periods.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), including Supplementary Material .04 (Customer's Investment Profile), .05 (Components of Suitability — reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability), and .07 (Customer-Directed Transactions); Regulation Best Interest, 17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii) (Care Obligation); FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (Non-Traditional ETFs — guidance on leveraged and inverse ETFs, their daily reset mechanisms, and suitability considerations); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 (Complex Products — heightened supervision requirements and reasonable-basis suitability for complex products including leveraged ETFs)

fact_pattern: In March 2023, financial advisor Derek Huang at Pemberton Wealth Partners recommended a reverse convertible note linked to three biotech stocks to his client, Miriam Castellano, age 58, a recently retired school principal with $1.2 million in retirement savings, moderate risk tolerance documented on her new account form, and a stated goal of generating income to supplement her pension. The note offered a 12.8% annualized coupon with a 6-month maturity and a 30% downside barrier on the worst-performing of the three underlying stocks. Derek conducted substantial research before making the recommendation: he reviewed the issuing bank's credit rating (A+), analyzed historical volatility of all three underlying biotech stocks over the past 5 years, ran Monte Carlo simulations suggesting only a 9% probability of breaching the barrier based on historical data, compared the coupon rate to comparable corporate bonds and CDs, and documented all of this in a detailed written memorandum in the client file. He also explained the product mechanics to Miriam in a 45-minute meeting, including the risk of receiving devalued shares if any stock fell below the barrier. Miriam signed a structured products disclosure acknowledging the risks. However, Derek did not specifically analyze Miriam's overall portfolio composition — at the time of the recommendation, she already held $180,000 in other structured notes (two autocallable notes and one principal-protected note), representing 15% of her total portfolio. The reverse convertible would add another $150,000, bringing her total structured product allocation to 27.5% of her retirement portfolio. Derek also did not consider that Miriam's documented moderate risk tolerance was based on a questionnaire completed during her initial onboarding two months earlier when she still expected to receive a $200,000 inheritance from her mother's estate, which she mentioned during onboarding. Between onboarding and the recommendation, Miriam's mother's estate entered probate litigation and the inheritance became uncertain, a fact Miriam mentioned casually during the 45-minute meeting but which Derek did not document or factor into his analysis.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation despite the extensive reasonable-basis research. Under FINRA Rule 2111, suitability has three components: reasonable-basis suitability, customer-specific suitability, and quantitative suitability. Derek likely satisfied reasonable-basis suitability by conducting thorough product-level research (Monte Carlo simulations, credit analysis, comparative yield analysis). However, he failed customer-specific suitability on multiple grounds. First, under FINRA Rule 2111.05(a), he had an obligation to consider the customer's overall portfolio and investment profile, not just the individual transaction. The 27.5% concentration in structured products — complex, illiquid instruments with embedded derivatives — is excessive for a 58-year-old moderate-risk retiree seeking income supplementation. Second, under FINRA Rule 2090 (Know Your Customer), Derek had a continuing obligation to know and update the essential facts about his customer. When Miriam disclosed the change in her inheritance expectation during the meeting, this constituted material information that could affect her risk capacity and overall financial situation. His failure to update her profile and reassess whether a moderate risk tolerance remained appropriate constitutes a violation. Additionally, FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 specifically addresses heightened suitability obligations for complex products like reverse convertibles, requiring firms and advisors to perform a 'reasonable diligence' review that goes beyond standard suitability, including understanding the product's risks relative to the specific customer's situation. The three-stock worst-of structure amplifies the risk significantly compared to single-stock reverse convertibles, and this elevated risk was not reconciled against the customer's changed financial circumstances. The fact that the client signed disclosures and received an explanation does not cure a suitability deficiency — informed consent does not substitute for suitability under FINRA rules.
why_adversarial: The extensive research documentation creates a strong impression of compliance. Most LLMs would focus on the thoroughness of Derek's reasonable-basis analysis (Monte Carlo simulations, credit review, comparisons, documentation, client disclosure) and conclude no violation occurred. The trap is that reasonable-basis suitability is only one of three components — the advisor can do perfect product-level research and still violate customer-specific suitability. The casual mention of the inheritance change is easy to overlook, and the concentration issue requires recognizing that the advisor must consider existing holdings, not just the individual recommendation. Many models also incorrectly treat signed risk disclosures as a safe harbor.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. The advisor conducted thorough research including Monte Carlo simulations, documented his analysis, explained the risks to the client in a detailed meeting, and obtained signed disclosures. The 9% barrier breach probability was reasonable, and the client was informed of and accepted the risks. The advisor went above and beyond in his due diligence.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — all three components: reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability; FINRA Rule 2090 (Know Your Customer); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 (Heightened Supervision and Suitability Obligations for Complex Products); FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-73 (Reverse Convertibles); Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) Rule 15l-1 under the Securities Exchange Act — Care Obligation requiring consideration of reasonably available alternatives and the customer's investment profile

fact_pattern: Gerald and Patricia Woodson, ages 67 and 64 respectively, are married retirees living in suburban Atlanta with combined retirement assets of $2.4 million. They maintain separate brokerage accounts at two different firms. Gerald has $1.4 million at Ridgeline Financial Services, managed by advisor Carla Resnick, invested as follows: $560,000 in diversified equity mutual funds (40%), $490,000 in investment-grade bond funds (35%), $210,000 in a real estate investment trust fund (15%), and $140,000 in cash equivalents (10%). Patricia has $1.0 million at Trident Capital Advisors, managed by advisor James Montague, invested as follows: $350,000 in an S&P 500 index fund (35%), $250,000 in a REIT-focused ETF (25%), $300,000 in a real estate limited partnership that invests in Southeast commercial properties (30%), and $100,000 in a money market fund (10%). Both advisors are aware the couple is married — it is noted in each client's account documentation. Neither advisor, however, has ever communicated with the other or requested details about the spouse's holdings at the other firm. In January 2024, James Montague recommended that Patricia invest an additional $100,000 from her money market fund into a new non-traded REIT focused on medical office buildings, citing strong demographic tailwinds from an aging population and a 6.5% distribution yield. James reviewed Patricia's account and noted that at his firm, she would have 65% in real estate-related investments after the purchase, which he flagged internally but justified in a memo stating that Patricia had indicated a 'high conviction' in real estate as an asset class, had prior experience as a licensed real estate agent before retirement, and had affirmatively requested more real estate exposure. Patricia's documented risk tolerance at Trident was 'moderate to aggressive' and her investment objective was listed as 'growth and income.' Looking at the couple's combined household, real estate exposure would rise from approximately $1.01 million to $1.11 million, or 46.25% of their total $2.4 million in combined assets. Gerald's advisor Carla had no involvement in or knowledge of James's recommendation.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, James Montague likely violated suitability requirements despite the client's request and experience. Under FINRA Rule 2111, a broker must have a reasonable basis to believe a recommendation is suitable based on the customer's investment profile, which includes the customer's other investments, financial situation and needs, and overall portfolio. FINRA has consistently interpreted 'other investments' to include investments held away when the advisor has knowledge or reason to know of them. James knew Patricia was married to Gerald and that Gerald maintained accounts elsewhere — this was documented. While James was not obligated to know the exact composition of Gerald's portfolio, the concentration analysis of Patricia's own account at Trident is itself problematic: 65% in real estate-related investments (including a non-traded REIT, which is illiquid) for a 64-year-old retiree with 'moderate to aggressive' risk tolerance is an excessive concentration even before considering household assets. FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-09 and subsequent guidance on non-traded REITs specifically note that many firms impose concentration limits of 10-15% of liquid net worth for non-traded REITs alone. The non-traded REIT plus the real estate LP would constitute 40% of Patricia's account in illiquid real estate vehicles. Furthermore, client-directed requests do not relieve the advisor of suitability obligations — under FINRA Rule 2111.05(c) and related interpretive guidance, a recommendation remains subject to suitability requirements even when it is consistent with a client's expressed preference. Patricia's real estate background may inform her knowledge but does not change her risk capacity as a retiree. However, Carla Resnick at Ridgeline did not violate any standard — she had no involvement in the recommendation and Gerald's account is reasonably diversified on its own.
why_adversarial: This scenario involves multiple traps. First, the multi-party structure across two firms creates confusion about whose obligation it is to monitor household concentration. Many LLMs will conclude that since James cannot control or fully know Gerald's holdings, he bears no responsibility for household-level concentration. Second, the client-direction trap — Patricia's explicit request for more real estate exposure, combined with her professional background as a real estate agent — creates a strong appearance that the advisor was simply following an informed client's wishes. Third, the question of whether James violated a standard requires knowing that suitability obligations are not excused by client requests and that concentration analysis of the client's own account is independently problematic even without the household view. Many models will focus on the household analysis (which is harder to establish as a violation) and miss the more straightforward account-level concentration issue.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. Patricia specifically requested additional real estate exposure, has professional experience in real estate, documented moderate-to-aggressive risk tolerance, and her advisor cannot reasonably be expected to monitor or control holdings at another firm managed by a different advisor. The client's autonomy and expertise should be respected, and James appropriately documented his rationale.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — customer-specific suitability component requiring analysis of customer's 'other investments,' financial situation, and investment profile; FINRA Rule 2111.05(c) (customer-requested transactions still subject to suitability when preceded by a recommendation); FINRA Rule 2090 (Know Your Customer); FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-09 (Suitability and Concentration Concerns for Non-Traded REITs); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 (Heightened Suitability for Complex Products including non-traded REITs); Regulation Best Interest Rule 15l-1 — Care Obligation requiring evaluation of concentration risks

fact_pattern: Margaret Dawson, age 72, retired schoolteacher with a $340,000 IRA and $1,200/month in Social Security income. She has moderate risk tolerance and needs her portfolio to generate approximately $1,400/month in supplemental income to cover living expenses. In March 2020, she walked into the offices of Bridgewater Capital Partners, a dually registered broker-dealer and investment adviser. She met with advisor Kevin Okafor. Kevin evaluated Margaret's situation and recommended she move her IRA into a fee-based advisory account charging 1.75% annually ($5,950/year) invested in a diversified portfolio of individual municipal bonds, Treasury securities, and two low-cost bond ETFs. The portfolio was designed to generate approximately $1,500/month in income with minimal trading expected — Kevin projected perhaps 2-3 trades per year for rebalancing. Margaret agreed. Over the next 30 months, Kevin executed exactly 4 trades total: two minor rebalancing trades and two bond reinvestments. The portfolio performed as expected, generating steady income. Margaret's all-in costs over 30 months totaled approximately $14,875 in advisory fees. Kevin had also considered but rejected a commission-based brokerage account where Margaret would have paid approximately $250 in total commissions for the same 4 trades over the same period, plus a $75 annual IRA custodial fee — totaling roughly $825. Kevin's internal notes state: 'Client prefers the comfort of ongoing advisory relationship and access to financial planning. Fee-based account appropriate.' Margaret never requested financial planning services and no financial plan was ever produced. Kevin did provide quarterly portfolio review calls lasting 5-10 minutes each.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation. This is a classic case of reverse churning — placing a client in a fee-based account where ongoing advisory fees vastly exceed what the client would pay in a commission-based account, without providing sufficient advisory services to justify the fee differential. Under Regulation Best Interest (Rule 15l-1 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934), the Cost component of the Care Obligation requires that the broker-dealer consider reasonably available alternatives and not place the financial interest of the firm ahead of the customer. The cost differential is staggering: approximately $14,875 vs. $825 over 30 months — the fee-based account cost roughly 18 times more. Additionally, under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 fiduciary duty (as articulated in SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau and the SEC's 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation), Kevin owed Margaret a duty of care requiring him to provide advice in her best interest, including evaluating whether the advisory fee was justified by services rendered. Kevin's internal notes claim Margaret 'prefers the comfort of ongoing advisory relationship,' but no financial plan was produced and the quarterly calls were perfunctory (5-10 minutes). This is insufficient to justify a $5,950 annual fee for a buy-and-hold bond portfolio. FINRA's Notice to Members 03-68 and Regulatory Notice 12-25 specifically flag the practice of placing accounts with low anticipated trading activity into fee-based programs as potentially unsuitable. The advisor's self-serving note about the client's 'preference' does not cure the violation because the advisor has an independent obligation to evaluate account type suitability regardless of client acquiescence.
why_adversarial: This is adversarial because on the surface, the advisor did everything 'right' — the portfolio was suitable, it performed well, the client was satisfied, income needs were met, and the advisor documented a rationale. Many LLMs would focus on the investment suitability (which is fine) and miss the account-type suitability issue. The trap is that the violation is not about WHAT was recommended but HOW the client was charged. The advisor's internal documentation creates a false paper trail suggesting client preference, which a general LLM might accept at face value. Additionally, the dual registration creates a rule_conflict: under the broker-dealer standard (Reg BI) the cost analysis is explicit, but under the investment adviser fiduciary standard, some might argue the client consented to the fee structure, creating tension between the two frameworks.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. The portfolio was appropriate for Margaret's risk tolerance and income needs, it performed as expected, the advisor documented his rationale for the fee-based account, and Margaret agreed to the arrangement. The 1.75% fee, while on the higher end, is within industry norms for advisory accounts.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), specifically the Care Obligation including cost considerations; Investment Advisers Act of 1940 fiduciary duty as interpreted in SEC Fiduciary Interpretation (IA-5248, June 2019); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) including account-type suitability; FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (FAQ on account type suitability); FINRA Notice to Members 03-68 (fee-based accounts)

fact_pattern: Dr. Samuel Pratt, age 55, an orthopedic surgeon earning $620,000 annually, opened a $1.2 million fee-based advisory account with Pinnacle Wealth Group in January 2021. His advisor, Rachel Stein, charged a 1.25% annual advisory fee ($15,000/year). Dr. Pratt's investment profile indicated aggressive growth, long time horizon (10+ years to retirement), and high risk tolerance. Rachel built a portfolio of 22 individual stocks, 4 sector ETFs, and 3 actively managed mutual funds (which carried their own expense ratios averaging 0.82%). Over the next two years (January 2021 through December 2022), Rachel executed 47 trades — roughly 2 trades per month — primarily rotating sector positions based on quarterly macro research her firm published. She also conducted two comprehensive annual financial planning reviews covering estate planning, tax optimization, and retirement projections. Each planning session lasted approximately 90 minutes and produced written reports. Dr. Pratt was generally pleased but never examined his fee statements closely. In January 2023, Dr. Pratt's accountant flagged that the combined cost of the advisory fee plus the embedded mutual fund expenses totaled approximately $24,840 per year (the 1.25% advisory fee plus approximately 0.82% weighted average expense ratio on the mutual fund portion, which comprised about $480,000 of the portfolio). The accountant noted that a commission-based account executing 47 trades over two years would have cost approximately $4,700 in commissions total, and if Rachel had used the same mutual funds' no-load share classes, the mutual fund expenses would have been roughly the same regardless of account type. Rachel's compliance file showed she had evaluated the account type at onboarding and noted: 'Client has complex financial planning needs; active management strategy with frequent rebalancing supports fee-based account.' Rachel did not document any comparison of projected costs between account types.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: This is technically compliant, though it represents a borderline case. Unlike a clear reverse churning scenario, Rachel Stein provided meaningful advisory services that could justify the fee-based account structure. She executed 47 trades over 24 months (approximately 2 per month), indicating active management rather than a dormant buy-and-hold strategy. She conducted two comprehensive financial planning sessions with written deliverables covering estate planning, tax optimization, and retirement projections — substantial services beyond mere portfolio management. Under Regulation Best Interest's Care Obligation (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), the advisor must consider costs among other factors, but cost is not the sole determinant. FINRA Rule 2111 account-type suitability similarly requires a reasonable basis for recommending a fee-based over commission-based account, but does not mandate that the fee-based account always be cheaper. The 47 trades at roughly $100 per trade equivalent in commissions would cost $4,700 over two years vs. $30,000 in advisory fees — a significant differential. However, the comprehensive financial planning services, active management strategy, and ongoing advisory relationship provide reasonable justification. The key deficiency is procedural: Rachel did not document a cost comparison between account types at onboarding, which represents a best practice gap under FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 and the Reg BI recordkeeping requirements (17 CFR § 240.15l-3). However, the absence of a documented cost comparison alone does not constitute a substantive violation if the account type was otherwise reasonably justified by the services provided. The embedded mutual fund expense issue is a separate consideration — under Reg BI's disclosure obligations, these layered costs should have been clearly disclosed, but the mutual fund expenses would exist regardless of account type (assuming the same funds were appropriate). The case is compliant, but the lack of documented cost comparison is a supervisory/compliance weakness that could become problematic in an examination.
why_adversarial: This scenario is designed to trap LLMs into calling it a violation based on the superficially alarming cost differential ($24,840/year vs. $4,700 in commissions). The accountant's flag creates a narrative frame suggesting wrongdoing. However, the scenario includes several facts that actually justify the fee-based account: substantial financial planning services, active trading, complex client needs, and a high-income client for whom the absolute fee amount is proportionally modest relative to income. The subtle trap is that the REAL deficiency (lack of documented cost comparison) is procedural rather than substantive — it's a compliance weakness but not necessarily a violation of the suitability or best interest standard itself. A general LLM would likely see the cost numbers, the accountant's concern, and immediately conclude 'violation,' missing the nuanced analysis of whether services rendered justified the fee structure.
common_wrong_answer: Yes, this is a violation. The fee-based account cost over five times more than a commission-based alternative would have, constituting reverse churning. The advisor failed to document a cost comparison, and the layered fees (advisory fee plus mutual fund expenses) demonstrate that the advisor prioritized her own compensation over the client's interests.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), Care Obligation and Cost considerations; Regulation Best Interest recordkeeping requirements (17 CFR § 240.15l-3); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), including account-type suitability; FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (FAQ regarding account type suitability); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); Investment Advisers Act of 1940 fiduciary duty per SEC Fiduciary Interpretation (Release No. IA-5248)

fact_pattern: Margaret Thornton, age 72, retired schoolteacher, opened a brokerage account with Apex Financial Group in March 2019. Her account documents listed her risk tolerance as 'conservative,' her investment objective as 'capital preservation and income,' annual income of $42,000 from Social Security and a small pension, liquid net worth of $310,000, and investment time horizon of 5-10 years. Her broker, David Kessler, placed her in a diversified portfolio of investment-grade corporate bonds, Treasury securities, and a conservative balanced mutual fund. In January 2020, Margaret's daughter, a successful tech entrepreneur, gifted Margaret $1.2 million in publicly traded tech stocks. Margaret called Kessler in February 2020 and told him she wanted to keep all of the tech stocks because 'my daughter knows what she's doing.' Kessler documented the call. He did not update Margaret's risk profile or account documentation to reflect the new asset composition or changed financial picture. In March 2020, during the COVID-19 market downturn, the tech stocks lost approximately $400,000 in value. Margaret complained. Kessler pointed out that he had not recommended the tech stocks, that Margaret had insisted on keeping them, and that the positions he had originally recommended actually performed well, losing less than 2% during the same period. Kessler's firm had transitioned from a commission-based suitability standard to a new compliance framework for all accounts effective June 30, 2020. Prior to that date, the firm operated under the older standard for existing accounts.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, Kessler likely violated his obligations, though the analysis depends on the applicable standard at the time. Prior to June 30, 2020, the account was governed by FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability). Under FINRA Rule 2111, there are three components: reasonable-basis suitability, customer-specific suitability, and quantitative suitability. The key issue is that FINRA Rule 2111 applies to 'recommended' transactions and investment strategies involving securities, including explicit recommendations to hold. Under FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25, a recommendation to 'hold' a security can trigger suitability obligations. When Margaret said she wanted to keep the tech stocks and Kessler simply acquiesced without analysis, he arguably made an implicit hold recommendation by failing to recommend she diversify or reduce concentration risk — especially given her documented conservative profile, age, income, and capital preservation objective. A portfolio suddenly concentrated ~80% in volatile tech stocks is fundamentally incompatible with a conservative, capital-preservation profile for a 72-year-old retiree. Moreover, FINRA Rule 4512 and related obligations required Kessler to make reasonable efforts to update customer account information, including financial situation and risk tolerance. Failing to update her profile after receiving $1.2 million in tech stocks — which radically changed her account composition — is itself a violation. Even though Reg BI (effective June 30, 2020) had not yet taken effect, the pre-existing suitability standard still required Kessler to address the dramatic mismatch between Margaret's stated profile and her actual holdings. The fact that he didn't recommend the initial purchase is not dispositive; his ongoing duty to address the hold and update account records means he violated FINRA Rules 2111 and 4512.
why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial for multiple reasons: (1) The temporal trap — the fact pattern carefully places the events before Reg BI's June 30, 2020 effective date, so an LLM might incorrectly apply Reg BI's care obligation rather than FINRA's suitability rule, or might think no standard applied during the transition. (2) The client-direction element creates a trap — many LLMs will conclude that because Margaret directed the hold and Kessler didn't recommend the purchase, he bears no responsibility. However, the hold recommendation doctrine under FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 and the account-update obligation under Rule 4512 still apply. (3) The original recommendations were sound, making it seem like Kessler did nothing wrong, when the violation relates to what he failed to do regarding the new positions and profile update.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. Kessler did not recommend the tech stocks — they were a gift from Margaret's daughter — and Margaret explicitly directed him to keep them. His original recommendations were conservative and appropriate. He documented her instructions. An advisor cannot be held responsible for unsolicited customer decisions to hold gifted securities.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), including the hold recommendation doctrine as clarified in FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25; FINRA Rule 4512 (Customer Account Information); FINRA Rule 2090 (Know Your Customer). Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) was not yet effective for the relevant period (effective June 30, 2020) but would impose even more explicit obligations regarding account monitoring and care.

fact_pattern: Evan Stratford, a registered representative at Coastal Securities LLC, was approached in August 2022 by a private real estate development firm, Horizon Realty Capital, seeking to raise $25 million through a private placement offering of limited partnership interests. The minimum investment was $100,000, with a 7-year lockup period, projected annual distributions of 8-10%, and an overall projected IRR of 15%. Stratford conducted extensive due diligence over six weeks: he reviewed the offering memorandum, financial projections, and independent appraisals of the three properties in the portfolio; he visited two of the three development sites; he met with the managing partners and reviewed their track record (12 prior funds, 9 profitable, 3 that returned less than invested capital); he consulted with a third-party due diligence firm that gave the offering a 'satisfactory' rating; he verified the developer's representations about zoning approvals and construction permits; and he reviewed audited financials from the sponsor's prior three funds. He documented all of this in a 40-page due diligence file. Starting in October 2022, Stratford recommended the offering to 14 clients. Among them was Client #7, Patricia Volkov, age 58, a recently divorced dental hygienist earning $78,000 per year. Volkov's updated account profile from September 2022 showed liquid net worth of $490,000, total net worth of $620,000 (including her home), investment objective of 'growth and income,' risk tolerance 'moderate,' and investment time horizon of '10+ years.' She had no prior experience with alternative investments or illiquid products. Her account held index mutual funds and a small allocation to high-yield bond funds. Stratford recommended she invest $100,000 — the minimum — representing approximately 20.4% of her liquid net worth. He explained the lockup period, the risks of real estate development, and the illiquid nature of the investment. Patricia signed all disclosure documents and acknowledged in writing that she understood the risks. Stratford also verified that Patricia met the accredited investor thresholds based on her net worth.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation at the customer-specific suitability level despite thorough reasonable-basis due diligence. Under FINRA Rule 2111 and Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), which was in effect by October 2022, Stratford had obligations at multiple levels. His reasonable-basis suitability (understanding the product) appears sound — the 40-page due diligence file, site visits, third-party review, and documentation are commendable and likely satisfy FINRA's expectations under Regulatory Notice 10-22 (guidance on private placements due diligence). However, customer-specific suitability is a separate and independent obligation. Allocating 20.4% of a client's liquid net worth to a single illiquid, 7-year lockup alternative investment is excessive for a 58-year-old moderate-risk investor with no alternative investment experience, earning $78,000 annually, who recently went through a divorce (suggesting potential future liquidity needs). Under Reg BI's Care Obligation (17 CFR § 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)), the broker must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to ensure the recommendation is in the customer's best interest, considering the customer's investment profile including financial situation, needs, and other securities held. FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-02 specifically warns about concentration in illiquid products and notes that even if a customer qualifies as an accredited investor, that status alone does not make the investment suitable. The fact that Patricia met accredited investor thresholds under Regulation D is irrelevant to suitability — accredited investor status is a securities law exemption for the issuer, not a suitability safe harbor for the broker. Additionally, her lack of experience with alternatives is a significant factor. While there is no bright-line concentration rule, FINRA enforcement actions have consistently found concentrations of 15-25%+ in illiquid alternatives problematic for moderate-risk clients, especially those approaching retirement with limited income. Stratford's excellent product-level diligence does not cure the customer-specific mismatch.
why_adversarial: This is a 'reasonable_basis_trap' because Stratford's product-level due diligence is genuinely exemplary — far exceeding what many advisors do. A general-purpose LLM will likely focus heavily on the extensive due diligence and conclude no violation occurred, conflating reasonable-basis suitability with customer-specific suitability. The trap is that these are independent requirements, and passing one does not cure a failure on the other. Additionally, LLMs commonly treat accredited investor qualification as dispositive of suitability, which is incorrect. The fact that all disclosures were made and Patricia signed acknowledgments adds another layer — many LLMs treat informed consent as a defense, when it is not under either FINRA suitability rules or Reg BI. The concentration percentage (20.4%) is in a gray zone that requires nuanced judgment rather than a clear bright-line rule.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. Stratford conducted exceptionally thorough due diligence on the offering, verified Patricia met accredited investor standards, fully disclosed the risks and illiquidity, obtained her written acknowledgment, and the investment aligned with her 10+ year time horizon and growth-and-income objective. The 8-10% projected distributions serve her income needs. His diligence exceeded industry norms.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest, 17 CFR § 240.15l-1, specifically the Care Obligation under § 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — all three components: reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability; FINRA Regulatory Notice 10-22 (due diligence obligations for private placements); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-02 (complex products and concentration risk); FINRA Rule 2090 (Know Your Customer); SEC Regulation D, Rule 501 (accredited investor definition — relevant but not a suitability safe harbor).

fact_pattern: Margaret Holloway, age 62, retired schoolteacher with $420,000 in savings, opened a brokerage account with Ridgeline Financial Services in March 2019. Her account opening documents listed her risk tolerance as 'moderate,' her investment objective as 'income with capital preservation,' and her investment time horizon as '10+ years.' Her advisor, Thomas Crane, built a portfolio of 60% investment-grade corporate bonds, 25% blue-chip dividend-paying equities, and 15% in a money market fund. In January 2020, Margaret's husband passed away. She inherited an additional $310,000 and rolled it into the same brokerage account. She met with Thomas in February 2020 and told him she wanted to 'keep everything the same — I trust your judgment and I just can't think about finances right now.' Thomas did not update any account documentation, did not reassess her risk profile, and simply invested the $310,000 inheritance using the same 60/25/15 allocation. In March 2020, during the COVID-19 market downturn, her equity holdings lost approximately $47,000 in value. Margaret filed a complaint in June 2020 alleging that Thomas should have reassessed her situation after her husband's death, that she was now solely dependent on these funds for retirement income, and that her actual risk tolerance had materially changed. Thomas's firm argues that (a) the customer explicitly directed him to keep the allocation the same, (b) the portfolio was objectively moderate and suitable for a moderate-risk investor, and (c) the customer's stated profile at account opening still governed. Notably, Ridgeline Financial Services had transitioned from the prior suitability framework to an enhanced standard for its broker-dealer operations effective June 30, 2020 — approximately four months after the contested investment of the inherited funds. The investments at issue were all made prior to June 30, 2020.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, Thomas Crane violated the applicable suitability standard even under the pre-Reg BI framework that applied before June 30, 2020. Under FINRA Rule 2111, which governed broker-dealer recommendations during this period, suitability has three components: reasonable-basis suitability, customer-specific suitability, and quantitative suitability.
