Customer-specific suitability requires that a recommendation be consistent with the customer's investment profile, which FINRA Rule 2111(a) defines as including, among other factors, the customer's 'other investments, financial situation and needs, tax status, investment objectives, investment experience, investment time horizon, liquidity needs, risk tolerance, and any other information the customer may disclose.' Critically, FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 clarifies that a broker's suitability obligation is an ongoing one when a broker makes a recommendation — and investing newly received inherited funds constitutes a new recommendation. When Margaret brought $310,000 in new assets, Thomas made a new recommendation by allocating those funds. At that point, he had an independent obligation to ensure the recommendation was suitable based on her current profile. Margaret's circumstances had materially changed: she lost a spouse (potential loss of social security survivor benefit considerations, emotional vulnerability, changed household income dynamics), she became solely dependent on these assets, and she explicitly stated she was in emotional distress ('I just can't think about finances right now'). FINRA has repeatedly emphasized that a customer's instruction to 'keep things the same' does not relieve a broker of the obligation to ensure suitability of a new recommendation. The fact that the customer directed the broker to maintain the allocation is not a defense under FINRA Rule 2111.07 (the customer-specific suitability safe harbor for unsolicited transactions) because Thomas was actively recommending how to invest new money — this was a solicited recommendation, not an unsolicited customer-directed trade. Even though Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) had not yet taken effect (its compliance date was June 30, 2020), the FINRA suitability standard independently required Thomas to update Margaret's profile and reassess whether the allocation was appropriate for her changed circumstances. The firm's argument that the prior profile 'still governed' is incorrect; a material life event such as a spouse's death triggers a reassessment obligation when new recommendations are being made. The portfolio allocation itself (25% equities) might have been suitable for the original profile, but without proper reassessment, there was no reasonable basis to conclude it remained suitable for her changed circumstances.
why_adversarial: This scenario creates a temporal trap: the transition date to Regulation Best Interest (June 30, 2020) occurred after the contested conduct, tempting an LLM to either (a) incorrectly apply Reg BI retroactively and analyze under the wrong standard, or (b) conclude that because the 'enhanced' standard hadn't taken effect yet, the advisor's conduct was compliant under the 'lesser' prior standard. Additionally, the client direction trap — Margaret explicitly told Thomas to keep everything the same — tempts the LLM to invoke the unsolicited transaction safe harbor, which does not apply here because investing new inherited funds constitutes a new recommendation. A general LLM might also underestimate the significance of a material life event triggering reassessment obligations even under the older suitability framework.
common_wrong_answer: No violation — the customer explicitly directed the advisor to keep the same allocation, the portfolio was objectively moderate and consistent with her stated risk profile, and the enhanced best interest standard had not yet taken effect. The advisor reasonably relied on the customer's stated preferences and existing profile.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), including FINRA Rule 2111(a) customer-specific suitability component; FINRA Rule 2111.07 (safe harbor for unsolicited transactions — inapplicable here); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (guidance on suitability obligations including updated customer profiles); FINRA Rule 2090 (Know Your Customer). Note: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) compliance date of June 30, 2020 was not yet in effect for the transactions at issue, so FINRA Rule 2111 is the controlling standard.

fact_pattern: David Castillo, age 45, is a senior software engineer at NovaTech Industries, a publicly traded technology company with a market capitalization of $38 billion. David earns $285,000 per year in salary and receives approximately $200,000 annually in restricted stock units (RSUs) that vest over four years. By April 2022, David's total liquid investment portfolio at Meridian Wealth Advisors was worth $1.8 million. Of that, $1.1 million (approximately 61%) was in NovaTech stock — $650,000 from vested RSUs he had never sold and $450,000 he had purchased on the open market over several years at the recommendation of his advisor, Rachel Fontaine. Rachel had prepared a detailed 14-page investment analysis in January 2022 supporting the NovaTech position. The analysis included: (1) a discounted cash flow model projecting 18% annual revenue growth based on NovaTech's entry into cloud infrastructure, (2) a comparison to five peer companies showing NovaTech trading at a 15% discount to sector average price-to-earnings ratio, (3) an assessment of NovaTech's balance sheet showing $4.2 billion in cash reserves and minimal debt, (4) a bullish consensus from 22 of 26 Wall Street analysts covering the stock, and (5) a note that David's total net worth including his home equity ($600,000), 401(k) ($430,000 — also 40% in NovaTech stock through the company plan), and his wife's separate retirement accounts ($220,000) was approximately $3.05 million. Rachel documented that she discussed concentration risk with David on three separate occasions (October 2021, January 2022, and March 2022) and that David each time declined to reduce his NovaTech position, stating he had 'deep conviction' in the company's prospects and 'understood the company better than any analyst.' Rachel's notes from the January 2022 meeting state: 'Client acknowledges concentration risk. Reviewed diversification alternatives including collars and exchange funds. Client declined all strategies. Recommended maintaining current position given strong fundamental analysis and client's informed preference.' In November 2022, NovaTech's stock dropped 44% after a failed product launch and an accounting restatement. David's NovaTech holdings fell from $1.1 million to approximately $616,000, and his 401(k) NovaTech holdings dropped proportionally. David filed a complaint alleging Rachel should never have allowed — let alone recommended — the open-market purchases that brought his concentration to 61%, and that her analysis, while detailed, failed to adequately account for the compounding concentration risk from his RSUs, ongoing salary dependence on NovaTech, and the 401(k) NovaTech allocation.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer:
Yes, Rachel Fontaine likely violated the applicable suitability and best interest standards despite her extensive research and documentation. The analysis must consider two distinct issues: (1) the $450,000 in open-market purchase recommendations, and (2) the implicit recommendation to hold the existing $650,000 RSU position without diversification.

Under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), which was in effect by the time of Rachel's January 2022 analysis and March 2022 recommendations, a broker-dealer must act in the retail customer's best interest at the time a recommendation is made, without placing her own interest ahead of the customer's. The Care Obligation under Reg BI requires the advisor to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making recommendations, considering the customer's investment profile including their full financial picture.

Rachel's fundamental analysis of NovaTech as a standalone security may have satisfied reasonable-basis suitability (the first prong of the old FINRA Rule 2111 framework, which remains relevant as FINRA Rule 2111 still applies alongside Reg BI). However, she failed the customer-specific component. The critical deficiency is that Rachel's analysis did not holistically account for David's total NovaTech exposure. When properly calculated, David's NovaTech concentration was not merely 61% of his brokerage account — it was far more severe: $1.1 million (brokerage) + approximately $172,000 (40% of $430,000 in his 401(k)) = $1.272 million in NovaTech stock out of $3.05 million total net worth, or approximately 42% of total net worth. But this understates the true risk because David's salary ($285,000/year) and future RSU grants ($200,000/year) also depend on NovaTech's success, creating massive correlated human-capital risk. A severe NovaTech decline could simultaneously destroy his portfolio value, reduce or eliminate his RSU income, and potentially threaten his employment. FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 specifically addresses concentration risk and states that 'reasonable-basis suitability requires a firm to perform adequate due diligence to understand the risks and rewards of a recommended security or strategy,' and that customer-specific suitability requires consideration of the customer's entire financial picture, including holdings at other firms and correlated exposures. Rachel acknowledged the concentration but then recommended maintaining it — and worse, she was the one who recommended the $450,000 in open-market purchases that built the concentration in the first place. Her documentation of client conversations about concentration risk, while helpful procedurally, does not insulate her from liability because she affirmatively recommended purchases that increased concentration to a clearly excessive level. Under Reg BI, the fact that a customer declines to diversify does not relieve the advisor of the obligation not to recommend further concentration-increasing purchases. Rachel should have, at minimum, stopped recommending additional open-market NovaTech purchases once the concentration became excessive. Her 14-page analysis, while thorough on company fundamentals, reflects a reasonable-basis analysis that was disconnected from the customer-specific suitability failure — a textbook 'reasonable basis trap' where the quality of the security-level research masks the inappropriateness of the recommendation for this specific customer.
why_adversarial: This scenario is designed to trick LLMs in several ways. First, the advisor's extensive documentation and detailed 14-page analysis create a strong appearance of diligence and compliance — most LLMs will be impressed by the thoroughness and conclude no violation occurred. Second, the client repeatedly declined diversification and expressed informed conviction, which tempts the LLM to apply a 'client autonomy' defense. Third, the advisor documented three separate conversations about concentration risk, which looks like exemplary compliance procedure. However, the trap is that good documentation of a bad recommendation is still a violation. The advisor affirmatively recommended the open-market purchases that built the concentration — this is not a case where the client independently accumulated stock. The 14-page analysis demonstrates reasonable-basis suitability for NovaTech as a security, but completely fails customer-specific suitability when the client's total economic exposure to NovaTech (stock + RSUs + salary + 401(k)) is considered. A general LLM will likely focus on the procedural compliance and miss the substantive violation.
common_wrong_answer: No violation — the advisor conducted thorough fundamental research, documented concentration risk discussions on three occasions, presented diversification alternatives including collars and exchange funds, and the client made an informed decision to maintain the position. The advisor's 14-page analysis demonstrated reasonable diligence, and the client's superior knowledge of the company as an employee justified the conviction. The subsequent stock decline was caused by unforeseeable events (failed product launch and accounting restatement), not an unsuitable recommendation.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), including the Care Obligation (§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), including reasonable-basis suitability and customer-specific suitability components; FINRA Rule 2111(b) (investment profile factors); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 (guidance on concentration risk and complex products suitability); FINRA Rule 2090 (Know Your Customer); SEC Reg BI Adopting Release (June 2019) discussion of recommendations to hold and implicit hold recommendations.

fact_pattern: Margaret Thornton, age 62, is a retired schoolteacher with a $420,000 rollover IRA and a modest $1,800/month pension. She has no other liquid savings. Her stated investment objective is 'income with moderate growth' and her risk tolerance is 'moderate.' Her investment time horizon is listed as 10-15 years. In March 2019, her broker-dealer registered representative, David Kowalski, recommended she invest $84,000 (20% of her IRA) into a non-traded Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) that pays a 6.5% distribution, with an expected hold period of 7-10 years and no secondary market. Kowalski conducted a thorough due diligence review of the REIT sponsor, examined the offering memorandum, verified the REIT's underlying commercial real estate portfolio was diversified across 14 properties in 8 states, and confirmed the distribution coverage ratio was healthy at 1.2x. He documented all of this analysis in his file. His firm's written supervisory procedures at the time set a 25% maximum concentration limit for illiquid alternative investments in retirement accounts. Margaret signed all disclosure documents acknowledging the illiquid nature of the investment and the risks involved. In June 2020, Kowalski moved to a new firm that was a registered investment adviser. He brought Margaret's account with him. At the new firm, acting now as an investment adviser representative, he conducted an annual review in January 2021 and recommended Margaret maintain her position in the non-traded REIT, noting the distribution was still being paid and the sponsor had not announced any liquidity event concerns. Margaret's financial situation had not materially changed. By late 2022, the REIT suspended distributions and announced a 30% write-down of net asset value due to commercial real estate market deterioration.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: The initial 2019 recommendation was likely compliant under the suitability standard that applied to Kowalski as a broker-dealer registered representative. The 20% allocation was within his firm's 25% concentration limit for illiquid alternatives in retirement accounts, his due diligence on the product was thorough and documented, and the investment's income characteristics aligned with Margaret's stated objectives. However, the January 2021 recommendation to MAINTAIN the position is where the violation likely occurred. By that time, Kowalski had moved to a registered investment adviser and was subject to the fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, which imposes a duty of care and duty of loyalty. Additionally, Regulation Best Interest (effective June 30, 2020) had taken effect, though as an IAR he was now under the higher fiduciary standard rather than Reg BI. Under the fiduciary standard, the 2021 'hold' recommendation was itself an affirmative recommendation requiring full analysis. The duty of care required Kowalski to consider whether a 62-year-old retiree (now 64) with no other liquid savings and reliance on her IRA for future income should maintain 20% of her retirement in an illiquid investment with no secondary market, especially given the COVID-19 pandemic's emerging impact on commercial real estate. The fiduciary duty requires ongoing monitoring and a duty to update advice — not merely confirming the distribution was still being paid. He should have evaluated whether the risk profile of the REIT had changed given macroeconomic conditions, whether Margaret's advancing age warranted reducing illiquid exposure, and whether the concentration in an illiquid product remained prudent given her total financial picture. The failure to recommend reducing or exiting the position (or at minimum documenting a robust analysis of why maintaining was in her best interest under the heightened fiduciary standard) constitutes a violation of the fiduciary duty of care.
why_adversarial: This is a temporal trap because two different standards applied at different points in the timeline. Most LLMs will either (1) evaluate the entire fact pattern under the suitability standard and find no violation because the 20% was within limits and due diligence was done, or (2) evaluate everything under the fiduciary standard and incorrectly find the initial 2019 recommendation was also a violation. The key trap is recognizing that Kowalski changed his registration from a broker-dealer rep to an IAR, shifting the applicable standard, and that the 2021 'hold' recommendation — which seems innocuous — was the actual point of violation under the higher fiduciary duty. Many models miss that a 'hold' recommendation triggers fiduciary analysis.
common_wrong_answer: No violation occurred. The advisor conducted thorough due diligence, stayed within the firm's 25% concentration limit, the investment matched the client's income objective, and the client signed all disclosures. The subsequent loss was due to unforeseeable market conditions, not advisor misconduct.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) applied to the March 2019 recommendation as a broker-dealer registered representative; Investment Advisers Act of 1940 Sections 206(1) and 206(2) fiduciary duty applied to the January 2021 recommendation as an investment adviser representative; SEC Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers (IA Release No. 5248, June 2019) clarifying the duty of care includes duty to provide advice, duty to seek best execution, and duty to monitor; Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) effective June 30, 2020 is relevant context but superseded by the higher fiduciary standard once Kowalski became an IAR.

fact_pattern: Carlos Reyes, age 45, is a senior software engineer at a publicly traded technology company earning $310,000 per year. He has a brokerage account with $1.1 million at a full-service broker-dealer, managed by his financial advisor, Stephanie Park. Carlos also holds approximately $2.8 million in vested company stock options and restricted stock units outside this brokerage account, which Stephanie is aware of because Carlos disclosed it on his new account form and has discussed it multiple times. Carlos's account form lists his risk tolerance as 'aggressive,' his investment experience as 'extensive,' and his time horizon as '20+ years.' In February 2023, Carlos instructed Stephanie to invest $770,000 of his $1.1 million brokerage account — roughly 70% — into a diversified technology sector ETF that holds over 300 technology stocks (no single holding exceeds 4%). Carlos told Stephanie, 'I know tech inside and out, I believe in the sector long-term, and I want concentrated tech exposure.' Stephanie noted his instruction in her file. She did not push back or discuss how this allocation, combined with his $2.8 million in company tech stock, would result in approximately 92% of his total known investable assets ($3.57 million of $3.9 million) being concentrated in the technology sector. She executed the trade as directed. She did not document any analysis of his total financial picture including the company stock. Her firm does not have a specific written policy setting a maximum sector concentration percentage.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation despite the client's explicit direction. Under Regulation Best Interest's Care Obligation (17 CFR § 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)), a broker-dealer and its associated persons must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill when making a recommendation, and this includes when a customer requests a specific transaction. While the ETF itself is diversified, the Care Obligation requires consideration of the customer's full investment profile. Stephanie knew about the $2.8 million in company tech stock. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) and its three components — reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability — the customer-specific obligation requires that the advisor have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is suitable for the particular customer based on that customer's investment profile, which explicitly includes the customer's 'other investments' per FINRA Rule 2111.04. Even though Carlos directed the trade, FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 clarifies that a broker cannot simply rely on a customer's stated wishes to override suitability concerns. The advisor has an independent obligation to evaluate suitability. Furthermore, under Reg BI's Care Obligation, the advisor must consider 'reasonably available alternatives.' Stephanie should have (1) discussed the total portfolio concentration risk — 92% in one sector — including the correlation between his employment income, company stock, and proposed investment, (2) recommended alternatives or a more balanced allocation, and (3) if Carlos still insisted, documented a thorough analysis showing she fulfilled her obligations and considered the holistic picture before proceeding. Her complete failure to analyze or document the total concentration, or even raise the issue with Carlos, constitutes a violation of both the Care Obligation under Reg BI and customer-specific suitability under FINRA Rule 2111.
why_adversarial: This scenario is designed to trap LLMs for several reasons: (1) The client explicitly directed the trade, which many models interpret as absolving the advisor of responsibility; (2) The product itself — a diversified ETF holding 300+ stocks — appears reasonable and non-concentrated in isolation; (3) The client has aggressive risk tolerance and extensive experience, which seems to support the allocation; (4) There is no firm-specific policy being violated. The trap is that the advisor KNEW about the outside holdings and failed to consider them in evaluating the total concentration risk. Many LLMs incorrectly conclude that client-directed trades with sophisticated clients cannot be violations.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. Carlos is a sophisticated, experienced investor with an aggressive risk tolerance who explicitly directed the trade. The ETF itself is well-diversified with 300+ holdings. The advisor is not responsible for assets held outside the brokerage account, and the client's clear instructions relieve the advisor of liability. Additionally, the firm had no concentration policy that was breached.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest Care Obligation (17 CFR § 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B)); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), particularly customer-specific suitability; FINRA Rule 2111.04 (defining investment profile to include 'other investments'); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (clarifying that customer direction does not eliminate suitability obligations); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55 (discussing concentration as a suitability consideration); Reg BI Adopting Release (SEC Release No. 34-86031) discussing the requirement to consider the customer's existing investment profile including known outside holdings.

fact_pattern: Margaret Holloway, age 62, is a retired schoolteacher with a $340,000 IRA rollover from her pension. Her stated investment objective is 'income with moderate growth,' her risk tolerance is moderate, her time horizon is 15-20 years, and she has limited investment experience. In March 2023, her advisor, Daniel Prescott at Meridian Wealth Partners, recommended she invest across a diversified portfolio of mutual funds. The allocation was as follows: $85,000 into the Broadmark Core Bond Fund (Class A shares, 4.25% front-end load), $85,000 into the Pinnacle Equity Income Fund (Class A shares, 5.50% front-end load), $85,000 into the Sentinel Balanced Growth Fund (Class A shares, 5.75% front-end load), and $85,000 into the Redwood International Equity Fund (Class A shares, 5.25% front-end load). The weighted average front-end load across the portfolio was approximately 5.19%. Daniel earned a total commission of approximately $17,646. Each fund individually had strong 5-year and 10-year track records and Morningstar ratings of 4 or 5 stars. The expense ratios for the Class A shares, after the load, ranged from 0.62% to 0.88% annually. Meridian's platform also offered institutional-class and no-load equivalents of three of the four funds, with expense ratios between 0.35% and 0.55%, which were available for accounts over $100,000. Daniel documented in his notes that he selected Class A shares because 'the breakpoint at $250,000 in the Pinnacle fund family would have required concentrating assets, which would reduce diversification,' and that 'Class A shares have lower ongoing expenses than Class C shares.' He did not document any comparison to the no-load or institutional share classes available on the platform. Margaret's account statement showed the portfolio value dropped to approximately $322,354 on day one after loads were deducted. Margaret did not complain and was satisfied with the fund selections.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation. While Daniel Prescott's fund selections were individually suitable in terms of investment objectives, risk profile, and diversification, he failed to consider reasonably available lower-cost alternatives — specifically the institutional-class and no-load share classes available on his own firm's platform. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), the quantitative suitability component and reasonable-basis analysis require that the advisor consider cost as a factor. More critically, under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), which was fully effective as of June 30, 2020 and therefore applicable to this March 2023 transaction, the Care Obligation (17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)) requires that the broker-dealer exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand available alternatives and make a recommendation that does not place the financial interest of the broker ahead of the customer. The Care Obligation specifically requires evaluating reasonably available alternatives, including cost. The fact that Class A shares have lower ongoing expenses than Class C shares is a red herring — the relevant comparison under Reg BI is against the institutional and no-load share classes that were available on the same platform for accounts of this size. The $17,646 in upfront commissions, representing 5.19% of the portfolio, significantly impacted a retirement account for a 62-year-old moderate-risk investor when materially cheaper alternatives existed on the same platform. Daniel's documented rationale addressed breakpoints and Class C comparisons but entirely failed to address the no-load/institutional share class comparison, which is the critical cost analysis required. Additionally, under Reg BI's Conflict of Interest Obligation, the compensation differential between load and no-load shares creates a conflict that must be disclosed and mitigated. The absence of any documented consideration of lower-cost alternatives available on the firm's own platform constitutes a failure of the Care Obligation even though the underlying investment selections were sound.
why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial because the advisor appears to have done many things right: diversified portfolio, strong fund selections, documented rationale mentioning breakpoints, correctly noted Class A is cheaper than Class C long-term, and the client is satisfied. A general LLM might focus on the individual fund suitability and the advisor's documented reasoning and conclude compliance. The trap is that the relevant comparison under Reg BI is not Class A vs. Class C, but Class A vs. the no-load/institutional share classes available on the same platform. Many LLMs would not recognize that the Care Obligation requires evaluating reasonably available alternatives including different share classes, and that the advisor's documented rationale, while partially correct, is fatally incomplete because it omits the most important comparison.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. The advisor selected well-rated, diversified funds appropriate for the client's objectives and risk tolerance. He documented his reasoning for selecting Class A shares over Class C shares and considered breakpoint implications. The weighted average load of 5.19% is within normal industry ranges for Class A shares. The client was satisfied with the recommendations.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), 17 CFR 240.15l-1, specifically the Care Obligation (17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(A)-(C)) requiring reasonable diligence, care, and skill in evaluating reasonably available alternatives including cost; the Conflict of Interest Obligation (17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(iv)); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) including reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability components; FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55 (guidance on suitability obligations regarding cost considerations); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision) regarding the firm's obligation to review share class recommendations.

fact_pattern: Victor Langston, age 45, is a senior software engineer at Helios Technologies, a publicly traded cloud computing company. His total net worth is approximately $3.8 million, of which $2.1 million consists of vested Helios stock and options acquired through his employment compensation over 12 years. His remaining assets include $900,000 in a 401(k) diversified across index funds, $500,000 in a joint brokerage account with his wife, and $300,000 in home equity. In January 2024, Victor opened a new advisory account at Sterling Financial Group with advisor Rachel Sung. During the onboarding process, Victor completed a detailed investor profile: his risk tolerance was marked as 'aggressive,' his investment objective was 'growth,' his time horizon was '20+ years,' his annual household income was $475,000, his liquidity needs were 'low,' and his investment experience was listed as 'extensive — actively manages own accounts for 15 years.' During their first meeting, Victor explicitly told Rachel: 'I believe Helios will triple in value over the next five years. I've been in this industry my whole career and I understand the business better than any analyst. I do not want to sell any Helios shares. I want you to manage the $500,000 joint brokerage account, but I'm also transferring my $2.1 million in Helios stock into this account for consolidated reporting. Do not sell the Helios stock under any circumstances.' Rachel documented this conversation in her CRM notes, had Victor sign a letter acknowledging his desire to maintain the concentrated Helios position, and coded the Helios shares as 'unsolicited/client-directed hold.' She then managed the $500,000 in diversified assets, investing them across a mix of growth ETFs and individual stocks across multiple sectors. Over the next six months, Helios stock appreciated 18%, bringing Victor's total Helios position to approximately $2.48 million, representing roughly 63% of his total net worth. Rachel sent quarterly performance reports that clearly showed the concentration percentage. At no point did Rachel recommend selling, hedging, or otherwise reducing the Helios concentration. She did not discuss protective put options, exchange funds, charitable remainder trusts, or any other concentration risk mitigation strategies. When asked at a compliance review why she hadn't addressed the concentration, Rachel stated: 'The client gave explicit instructions not to touch the Helios stock. I respected his wishes and focused on managing the assets he wanted me to manage.'
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation despite the client's explicit instructions. When Rachel Sung accepted the $2.1 million Helios position into her advisory account — even for 'consolidated reporting' — the entire account including the Helios shares fell within the scope of her advisory relationship and fiduciary duties. Under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Section 206(1) and 206(2), an investment adviser owes a fiduciary duty to clients that cannot be waived simply because the client expresses a preference. Under Regulation Best Interest (if applied at the broker-dealer level), the Care Obligation requires that the advisor consider the customer's full financial profile including concentration risk. Even if the Helios shares were coded as 'unsolicited,' once they were held within the advisory account, the advisor had an ongoing duty to monitor and advise on the entire portfolio. FINRA Rule 2111 and its supplementary materials (FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55) clarify that a firm cannot disclaim suitability obligations merely by labeling transactions or positions as unsolicited, particularly when the position is held within a managed or advisory account. The critical violation is not that Rachel failed to force-sell the Helios stock — she cannot override client instructions — but that she completely failed to advise, recommend, or even discuss concentration risk mitigation strategies. An advisor's obligation includes providing informed advice about risks, even when the client may reject that advice. Rachel should have: (1) formally documented a recommendation to reduce or hedge the concentration with specific strategies such as protective puts, collars, systematic diversification, exchange funds, or 10b5-1 plans; (2) explained the specific risks of single-stock concentration including company-specific risk, sector risk, and the correlation between Victor's employment income and his investment portfolio (dual concentration risk); (3) if Victor declined all mitigation strategies, documented his informed refusal after receiving the recommendation. Simply respecting the client's initial instruction without ever providing professional advice about the concentration risk is a failure of the advisor's core duty. The client direction defense fails here because the advisor never fulfilled the prerequisite obligation of actually advising the client about the risks and alternatives before accepting the client's direction as final.
why_adversarial: This is a sophisticated client-direction trap. The client is wealthy, experienced, aggressive in risk tolerance, has a long time horizon, and gave clear written instructions. Many LLMs will apply a straightforward 'client autonomy' analysis and conclude that an experienced, high-net-worth, aggressive investor can choose to hold a concentrated position, especially when the advisor documented the client's wishes and obtained a signed acknowledgment. The trap is that accepting assets into an advisory account creates ongoing advisory obligations that go beyond simply following client instructions. The violation is not about overriding the client's wishes — it's about the complete absence of any advisory discussion, recommendation, or risk disclosure regarding concentration. Most general LLMs do not distinguish between 'respecting client instructions' and 'failing to advise before accepting client instructions as final.'
common_wrong_answer: No violation. Victor is an experienced, high-net-worth, aggressive investor who gave explicit written instructions not to sell his Helios stock. The advisor documented the conversation, obtained a signed acknowledgment, properly coded the position as client-directed, and competently managed the assets Victor asked her to manage. The advisor cannot force a client to sell their own stock, and the client's profile (aggressive risk tolerance, long time horizon, high income, extensive experience) supports the ability to hold a concentrated position.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Sections 206(1) and 206(2) (fiduciary duty); SEC Interpretive Release IA-1092 (fiduciary obligations of investment advisers); Regulation Best Interest, 17 CFR 240.15l-1, Care Obligation (if broker-dealer capacity); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) and supplementary material .05(c) regarding customer-directed transactions; FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-55 (guidance clarifying that suitability obligations attach to recommendations and that advisors cannot use unsolicited designations to avoid obligations in managed accounts); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision, requiring firms to monitor for concentration risk); SEC Staff Bulletin on Standards of Conduct (April 2022, discussing ongoing monitoring obligations in advisory accounts).

fact_pattern: Margaret Kowalski, age 58, worked as a school cafeteria manager earning $42,000 annually. She had a $190,000 rollover IRA at a broker-dealer after retiring from a previous school district. Her account documents listed her investment experience as 'limited — only savings accounts and CDs,' her risk tolerance as 'moderate,' her time horizon as '5-10 years,' and her investment objective as 'growth and income.' On May 15, 2020, her financial advisor, Derek Huang, recommended she invest $95,000 (50% of her IRA) into a non-traded Business Development Company (BDC) that paid an 8.5% distribution yield. The BDC invested in mezzanine debt of middle-market companies and had a 7-year expected holding period, no secondary market, a 10% early redemption penalty, and total upfront costs (selling commissions plus dealer manager fees plus organizational costs) of 11.5%. Derek completed a product-specific training module on BDCs, documented in a file memo that Margaret wanted higher income than CDs offered, and noted that the 8.5% yield met her 'income' objective. He also noted that her moderate risk tolerance supported the investment because the BDC's distributions had been consistent since its 2017 inception. Margaret signed a subscription agreement that included risk disclosures. On March 1, 2020 — just 10 weeks before the recommendation — Derek's firm had transitioned from the legacy suitability framework to a new standard requiring recommendations to be in the customer's best interest. Derek had attended a two-hour webinar on the new standard but continued using his old suitability checklists. In September 2022, the BDC suspended distributions and announced its estimated NAV had dropped 35%. Margaret filed a complaint saying she never understood the product and needed the money within five years for retirement living expenses.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, Derek Huang violated the applicable standard. The recommendation was made on May 15, 2020, which falls after the June 30, 2020 compliance date for Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) under the Securities Exchange Act Rule 15l-1. However, the firm's own transition occurred on March 1, 2020 — meaning the firm had already adopted Reg BI's framework ahead of the SEC compliance date. Under Reg BI's Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)), the broker must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making a recommendation, must understand the risks and rewards of the product, and must have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the customer's best interest given her specific investment profile. Even under the prior FINRA Rule 2111 suitability standard (which would have applied if the firm had not yet transitioned), the recommendation likely fails customer-specific suitability. Under FINRA Rule 2111.05(a), a complex product like a non-traded BDC requires heightened scrutiny. The concentration of 50% of Margaret's retirement assets in a single illiquid, complex product with an 11.5% cost load, a 7-year holding period, and a 10% early redemption penalty is inconsistent with her 5-10 year time horizon (which overlaps the lockup), her limited investment experience, her moderate risk tolerance, and her need for accessible retirement funds. Under Reg BI, the analysis is even more demanding: Derek needed to consider reasonably available alternatives. Lower-cost, liquid income-producing alternatives (e.g., bond funds, dividend equity funds) existed that would have met her income objective without illiquidity risk and excessive costs. His reliance on the old suitability checklists after the firm transitioned to Reg BI also represents a failure to apply the correct standard. The fact that Margaret signed risk disclosures does not cure the violation; under both FINRA Rule 2111 and Reg BI, the obligation rests on the advisor to make a suitable/best-interest recommendation regardless of customer consent. Additionally, FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 (heightened supervision for complex products) and FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (non-traded REITs/BDCs) impose additional expectations including reasonable-basis suitability analysis of the specific product's features relative to alternatives.
why_adversarial: The temporal trap is multi-layered: the SEC's Reg BI compliance date was June 30, 2020, so a model might conclude the old suitability standard applies to a May 2020 recommendation. But the firm voluntarily adopted Reg BI early on March 1, 2020, making the higher standard applicable. Even models that catch this might then struggle with whether the recommendation would have survived under the old suitability standard anyway (it wouldn't, due to concentration, illiquidity, and customer-specific factors). The fact that Derek completed product training, documented the recommendation rationale, and obtained signed disclosures creates a surface appearance of compliance that masks the substantive failures. A general LLM might focus on the signed disclosures and training documentation as evidence of compliance.
common_wrong_answer: No violation — Reg BI was not yet effective (its compliance date was June 30, 2020), and under the old suitability standard, Derek performed adequate due diligence by completing product training, documenting the rationale, and obtaining signed risk disclosures from Margaret, who voluntarily chose a higher-yielding product consistent with her stated income objective and moderate risk tolerance.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (SEC Rule 15l-1, 17 CFR § 240.15l-1), effective compliance date June 30, 2020 (but firm adopted early); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Rule 2111.05(a) (Recommended Strategies Involving Complex Products); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 (Complex Products and Heightened Supervision); FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (Non-Traded REITs); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor)

fact_pattern: Vincent DeLuca, age 34, was a software engineer earning $175,000 annually with a net worth of approximately $1.2 million (including home equity). He opened a self-directed brokerage account at a mid-size broker-dealer in January 2023. His new account form listed his investment experience as 'extensive — 12 years of active trading including options and micro-cap equities,' risk tolerance as 'aggressive,' and investment objective as 'speculation.' Vincent had previously held accounts at two discount brokerages where he actively traded low-priced securities. In February 2023, Vincent contacted his assigned registered representative, Alicia Montoya, and specifically requested to purchase 200,000 shares of GreenVolt Dynamics Corp., a company trading at $0.03 per share on the OTC Pink marketplace with the 'Limited Information' designation, for a total investment of $6,000. Vincent told Alicia he had done his own research, believed the company's new battery patent would drive the stock higher, and stated: 'I know penny stocks are risky — I've been trading them for years. Just put in the order.' Alicia reviewed Vincent's account profile, confirmed his aggressive risk tolerance and speculation objective, and noted his stated experience with micro-cap equities. She did not, however, provide Vincent with a penny stock risk disclosure document or obtain a signed penny stock suitability statement from him prior to executing the trade. She also did not make a written determination that the penny stock transaction was suitable for Vincent prior to the trade. Alicia executed the trade. The stock subsequently dropped to $0.005 per share. Vincent did not complain about the trade itself but the firm's compliance department flagged the transaction during a routine review.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, Alicia Montoya violated applicable requirements, but not on traditional suitability grounds — the violation is procedural under the penny stock rules. Under SEC Rule 15g-2 (17 CFR § 240.15g-2), before effecting a transaction in a penny stock (defined under Exchange Act Section 3(a)(51) and Rule 3a51-1 as an equity security trading below $5 per share that does not meet certain exemptions), the broker must provide the customer with a risk disclosure document (the SEC-prescribed penny stock disclosure schedule) and obtain a signed and dated acknowledgment of receipt. Under SEC Rule 15g-9 (17 CFR § 240.15g-9), the broker must also obtain from the customer a signed, written suitability statement and make a written determination that the penny stock is suitable for the customer, considering the customer's financial situation, investment experience, and objectives. These are mandatory procedural requirements that apply regardless of whether the customer is sophisticated, experienced, or unsolicited in the request. The key nuance is that the exemption from penny stock rules for 'established customers' under Rule 15g-1(b) requires the customer to have held an account with the broker-dealer for at least one year or to have made three penny stock transactions of a certain size. Vincent opened his account in January 2023 and made the request in February 2023 — only about one month later — and this was his first penny stock transaction at this firm. His experience at other firms is irrelevant for the established customer exemption, which is firm-specific. Therefore, no exemption applies, and Alicia was required to comply with all penny stock disclosure and suitability documentation requirements. Under Reg BI (Rule 15l-1), which applies to all broker-dealer recommendations post-June 30, 2020, there is an additional layer: even though Vincent directed the trade, Alicia's execution without the required penny stock disclosures violates the Compliance Obligation component of Reg BI, which requires adherence to all applicable securities laws. Separately, under FINRA Rule 2111, the trade itself may not constitute a suitability violation given Vincent's profile — but the failure to comply with the penny stock procedural requirements is an independent violation under SEC Rules 15g-2 and 15g-9.
why_adversarial: This is a client direction trap combined with a knowledge trap. The customer is experienced, aggressive, knowledgeable about penny stocks, and explicitly requested the trade. Most general-purpose LLMs will focus on the traditional suitability analysis — where Vincent's profile (high income, aggressive risk tolerance, speculation objective, 12 years of experience, small position size relative to net worth) strongly suggests no suitability violation. The LLM will likely conclude 'no violation' because the trade fits the customer's profile and was unsolicited. However, the actual violation is the failure to comply with the mandatory penny stock disclosure and suitability documentation procedures under SEC Rules 15g-2 and 15g-9, which are absolute requirements that cannot be waived by customer sophistication or direction. The established customer exemption appears available but fails because Vincent's account was only one month old at this specific firm. This requires specific knowledge of the penny stock rules' procedural requirements and the firm-specific nature of the established customer exemption.
common_wrong_answer: No violation — Vincent was an experienced, aggressive investor who specifically requested the penny stock trade. The $6,000 investment represented only 0.5% of his net worth, his risk tolerance was aggressive, his objective was speculation, and he had 12 years of trading experience including micro-cap equities. The trade was consistent with his investment profile and was unsolicited, so neither suitability nor best interest requirements were violated.
applicable_standard: SEC Rule 15g-2 (17 CFR § 240.15g-2) — Penny Stock Risk Disclosure Document; SEC Rule 15g-9 (17 CFR § 240.15g-9) — Sales Practice Requirements for Penny Stocks; SEC Rule 15g-1 (17 CFR § 240.15g-1) — Exemptions for Established Customers; Exchange Act Section 3(a)(51) and SEC Rule 3a51-1 — Definition of Penny Stock; Regulation Best Interest (SEC Rule 15l-1) — Compliance Obligation; FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor)

fact_pattern: Marcus Devlin, age 58, retired school principal with a $340,000 rollover IRA and a $90,000 taxable brokerage account, met with his financial advisor, Brenda Kowalski, in January 2020. Marcus stated on his new account form that his investment objective was 'income with moderate growth,' his risk tolerance was 'moderate,' his annual income was $62,000 from pension and Social Security, his liquid net worth was $430,000, his time horizon was 10-15 years, and he had 'limited' investment experience consisting only of holding mutual funds in his employer retirement plan. Between February and May 2020, Brenda recommended and executed 14 separate purchases across 6 different over-the-counter bulletin board stocks, all trading below $0.50 per share, totaling $47,000 in Marcus's taxable brokerage account. Each stock was in a speculative micro-cap biotech or cannabis company with no revenue. Brenda prepared and provided Marcus with a written suitability disclosure document before each penny stock purchase. The document listed the risks associated with penny stocks, including potential total loss, lack of liquidity, wide bid-ask spreads, and susceptibility to manipulation. Marcus signed each disclosure. Brenda also documented in her notes that she verbally explained the speculative nature of each stock to Marcus and that he expressed understanding. Brenda had conducted her own research on each company, reviewing recent quarterly filings, and believed each had legitimate scientific or business prospects. By September 2020, the combined value of the six penny stock positions had declined to $8,200. Marcus filed a complaint alleging the recommendations were unsuitable. Brenda's firm argued that it had fully complied with all penny stock disclosure requirements and that the customer had been informed and consented.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation. The analysis involves two overlapping frameworks. First, regarding the penny stock suitability determination: Under the penny stock rules (Exchange Act Section 15(h) and SEC Rules 15g-1 through 15g-9), before effecting a penny stock transaction, a broker-dealer must make a written suitability determination that the penny stock is suitable for the customer based on the customer's financial situation and investment objectives, and obtain the customer's written agreement to the specific transaction. Brenda did comply with the procedural disclosure requirements. However, mere compliance with the penny stock disclosure procedures does not immunize the advisor from a separate, substantive suitability analysis. Second, and critically, the recommendations were subject to Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI, 17 CFR § 240.15l-1), which became effective June 30, 2020. For the trades executed before June 30, 2020, the FINRA Rule 2111 suitability standard applied. For any trades after that date, Reg BI's Care Obligation applied. Under both standards, the substantive analysis is the same here: a 58-year-old retiree with limited investment experience, moderate risk tolerance, an income objective, and a $430,000 liquid net worth should not have had $47,000 (approximately 52% of his taxable account, or about 11% of total liquid assets) concentrated in speculative penny stocks with no revenue. The customer-specific suitability prong of Rule 2111 and the Care Obligation of Reg BI both required that the recommendations be suitable for this specific customer, not merely disclosed. The penny stock disclosure documents satisfied a separate regulatory requirement but do not substitute for the suitability or best interest analysis. Additionally, FINRA Rule 2111's quantitative suitability component is implicated by the pattern of 14 purchases in 4 months in speculative securities. Brenda's reasonable-basis research does not cure the customer-specific unsuitability. The firm's defense confuses procedural penny stock compliance with substantive suitability, which are distinct obligations.
why_adversarial: This scenario is adversarial for two reasons. First, it creates a temporal trap: the trades span the transition from the FINRA Rule 2111 suitability standard to Regulation Best Interest (effective June 30, 2020), and a general LLM might apply only one standard or get the effective date wrong. Second, the firm's defense — that it fully complied with penny stock disclosure requirements — sounds compelling and creates a 'knowledge trap' within the temporal trap. Many LLMs would conflate penny stock disclosure compliance with suitability compliance, concluding that providing the written disclosures and obtaining signed acknowledgments was sufficient. In reality, the penny stock disclosure rules and the suitability/best interest obligation are separate and independent requirements.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely conclude there was no violation, reasoning that since Brenda provided all required penny stock risk disclosures, obtained written consent for each transaction, conducted her own research, and documented verbal explanations, she fulfilled her obligations. The LLM might state that the client was fully informed and voluntarily assumed the risk, making the recommendations compliant.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) for trades before June 30, 2020; Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), specifically the Care Obligation, for trades on or after June 30, 2020; SEC Rules 15g-1 through 15g-9 (Penny Stock Rules) under Exchange Act Section 15(h); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (guidance on suitability for complex and speculative products)

fact_pattern: Dr. Yolanda Reeves, age 44, an orthopedic surgeon earning $780,000 annually with a net worth of $4.2 million (excluding primary residence), maintained two brokerage accounts at two different firms. At Firm A, she worked with advisor Craig Tompkins, who managed her $1.8 million diversified portfolio consisting of equities, bonds, and index funds. At Firm B, she worked with advisor Natalie Sung, who managed a $600,000 account focused on alternative investments. In March 2023, Craig at Firm A recommended that Dr. Reeves invest $200,000 in a Regulation D private placement offering — a real estate development fund structured as a limited partnership with a 7-year lockup, minimum investment of $100,000, projected 12-15% annual returns, and distributions beginning in year 3. Craig verified that Dr. Reeves met the accredited investor threshold and reviewed the private placement memorandum with her. He documented that the investment represented approximately 4.8% of her total net worth, that she had a long time horizon, that she had prior experience with alternative investments through her Firm B account, and that her high income could absorb illiquidity risk. He noted her investment objectives for the Firm A account were 'growth' with 'aggressive' risk tolerance. What Craig did not know — and did not ask about — was that Natalie at Firm B had already invested $400,000 of Dr. Reeves's Firm B account into three other Regulation D private placements over the prior 18 months, all with lockup periods exceeding 5 years. Dr. Reeves did not volunteer this information. Including Craig's recommendation, Dr. Reeves's total private placement exposure would become $600,000, or approximately 14.3% of her net worth, with $600,000 in illiquid investments with multi-year lockups. Separately, Natalie's three prior recommendations at Firm B had each been individually analyzed and documented as suitable at the time. After the real estate fund Craig recommended suffered a capital call in 2024 and suspended distributions, Dr. Reeves filed complaints against both advisors, alleging that her aggregate private placement concentration was unsuitable.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Neither advisor violated suitability or best interest standards, though Craig's analysis was thin on one dimension. Under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) and FINRA Rule 2111, each advisor is obligated to make recommendations that are in the customer's best interest or suitable based on the information available to them about the customer, including information the customer provides and information reasonably obtainable. Craig at Firm A performed a customer-specific suitability analysis: he verified accredited investor status, assessed the investment against Dr. Reeves's stated net worth ($4.2 million), confirmed her aggressive risk tolerance and growth objective, considered her income's ability to absorb illiquidity, noted her experience with alternatives, and documented that the $200,000 investment was approximately 4.8% of her net worth. He did not know about the Firm B private placements. Under Reg BI's Care Obligation, Craig was required to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill, considering the customer's investment profile. A key question is whether Craig should have asked about holdings at other firms. Industry practice and regulatory guidance (including FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 and the Reg BI adopting release) encourage but do not mandate that advisors obtain a complete picture of a customer's outside holdings. Craig asked about her investment experience and was aware she had an account at another firm with alternative investments — but not the specific dollar amounts. Given that Dr. Reeves did not volunteer the information and Craig was not required to obtain account statements from Firm B, his analysis based on available information was reasonable. The $200,000 recommendation was approximately 11% of the Firm A account and 4.8% of total net worth as Craig understood it. Natalie at Firm B similarly performed individual suitability analyses on each of her three recommendations, documented them, and none individually was outsized. Each of Natalie's investments was roughly $133,000, or about 3.2% of net worth. No single advisor had knowledge of the aggregate concentration. While best practices would call for a more holistic conversation about outside illiquid holdings — and Craig's documentation could have been more robust in recording what he knew about Firm B holdings — the failure to discover a concentration across two independent firms, where the customer did not disclose it, does not constitute a violation of either advisor's suitability or best interest obligation under current standards. The complaint is understandable but does not establish a violation by either advisor.
why_adversarial: This multi-party scenario is adversarial because most LLMs will instinctively find a violation. The aggregate private placement concentration ($600,000, 14.3% of net worth, all illiquid) sounds problematic, and the instinct is to blame at least one advisor. However, the trap is that suitability and best interest obligations are assessed based on the information reasonably available to each individual advisor. Neither advisor had knowledge of the full picture, and there is no regulatory requirement that an advisor at one firm obtain detailed account statements from a customer's account at a competing firm. The LLM must resist the hindsight bias of seeing the full picture and instead evaluate each advisor's conduct based on what they knew. The case also tests whether the LLM understands that accredited investor status alone does not determine suitability but that it was just one factor Craig properly considered.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely conclude that Craig violated suitability standards because he failed to inquire about Dr. Reeves's holdings at Firm B before recommending the private placement, and that the aggregate 14.3% concentration in illiquid private placements was unsuitable. The LLM might also find that both advisors had a duty to understand the customer's complete financial picture across all accounts, and that their failure to do so constituted inadequate reasonable diligence.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1), specifically the Care Obligation; FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) including reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability components; FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-03 (Know Your Customer and Suitability); Regulation D (17 CFR §§ 230.501-506) for private placement framework and accredited investor standards; FINRA Notice to Members 10-22 (Private Placements due diligence guidance)

fact_pattern: In March 2024, Gerald Whitfield, age 58, opened a brokerage account with Meridian Securities, a small broker-dealer. Gerald had been a successful real estate developer for 30 years, had a liquid net worth of $4.2 million, and told his advisor, Rick Santana, that he wanted to allocate $200,000 to 'speculative plays' for potential high returns. Gerald had extensive experience trading large-cap equities and options over the past 15 years. He signed the new account form indicating a 'speculative' investment objective for this account, aggressive risk tolerance, and a 5-year time horizon. Rick recommended that Gerald purchase 400,000 shares of Viranova Corp (VRNA), a company trading at $0.38 per share on the OTC Pink marketplace. VRNA had a market capitalization of $6.1 million, no listed exchange, and had filed no reports with any federal regulatory body. Rick had researched the company, found it had revenue of $1.2 million, negative earnings, and limited public financial disclosures. Before executing the trade, Rick verbally told Gerald that VRNA was a penny stock, that it was highly speculative and illiquid, and that he could lose his entire investment. Gerald acknowledged the risks verbally and said, 'I've been around the block — just put the order in.' Rick executed the trade at $0.38 per share for a total of $152,000. Rick did not provide Gerald with any written risk disclosure document specific to penny stocks prior to the transaction, nor did he obtain a signed written agreement from Gerald specific to penny stock transactions. He also did not provide a written statement showing the market value and number of shares. Gerald's account application, however, contained a general risk disclosure paragraph covering speculative investments. Within four months, VRNA shares dropped to $0.02 and Gerald lost nearly all of his $152,000 investment.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation — but not primarily a traditional suitability violation. The critical issue is that Rick failed to comply with the specific procedural requirements mandated for penny stock transactions under Exchange Act Section 15(h) and SEC Rule 15g-2 through 15g-9 (the 'Penny Stock Rules'). These rules require that before effecting a transaction in a penny stock for a customer, the broker must: (1) approve the customer's account for penny stock transactions and obtain a signed, written agreement from the customer (Rule 15g-9(a)); (2) provide a standardized risk disclosure document (the 'penny stock disclosure schedule') and receive a signed and dated acknowledgment from the customer (Rule 15g-2); and (3) provide a written disclosure of the current bid/offer quotations and compensation information (Rule 15g-3, 15g-4, 15g-5). Verbal disclosure is insufficient. The general risk disclosure on the account application does not satisfy these penny-stock-specific requirements. There is an exemption under Rule 15g-1 for 'established customers' (those who have held an account for at least one year or have made three prior penny stock purchases), but Gerald opened his account in March 2024 and this was his first penny stock transaction, so that exemption does not apply. Additionally, under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) and its quantitative suitability component, and under Regulation Best Interest's Care Obligation (17 CFR 240.15l-1), recommending a single OTC Pink company with no regulatory filings, negative earnings, and a $6.1 million market cap for $152,000 — even to a wealthy, experienced investor — raises serious questions about reasonable-basis suitability, because the advisor could not form a reasonable belief that the security was suitable for anyone given the absence of reliable financial information. Gerald's wealth and risk tolerance do not excuse the broker from the penny stock procedural mandates, which are prophylactic rules designed to protect all investors regardless of sophistication.
why_adversarial: A general LLM is likely to focus entirely on traditional suitability analysis and conclude that the recommendation was suitable because Gerald was wealthy, experienced, had a speculative objective, and the position was a small percentage of his net worth. Most LLMs do not know the specific penny stock procedural requirements (Rules 15g-2 through 15g-9) that impose mandatory written disclosure obligations regardless of the customer's sophistication or suitability profile. The trap is that the suitability analysis — wealthy client, speculative objective, small allocation — looks clean, but the penny stock rules create independent procedural violations that most general AI models will miss entirely.
common_wrong_answer: No violation. Gerald was a wealthy, experienced investor with a speculative investment objective. The $152,000 investment represented only about 3.6% of his liquid net worth. Rick verbally disclosed the risks, and Gerald voluntarily accepted them. The recommendation was suitable given the customer's profile.
applicable_standard: Exchange Act Section 15(h); SEC Rules 15g-1 through 15g-9 (Penny Stock Rules); SEC Rule 15g-2 (Risk Disclosure Document requirement); SEC Rule 15g-9 (Sales Practice Requirements — written suitability determination and signed customer agreement for non-established customers); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability — reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability); Regulation Best Interest, 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Care Obligation and Compliance Obligation); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade)

fact_pattern: Dorothy Kessler, age 72, retired schoolteacher, visited Harborview Financial Services in January 2024 seeking help with her $680,000 retirement portfolio, which consisted entirely of bank CDs earning 4.8% APY. Dorothy's sole income was Social Security of $2,400/month and her CD interest, which together covered her $4,100/month living expenses. She told her advisor, Natalie Chen, that she was 'very conservative,' that she 'could not afford to lose principal,' and that she needed 'reliable monthly income to pay bills.' Her account documents listed her investment objective as 'income,' risk tolerance as 'conservative,' time horizon as '10+ years' (life expectancy), and annual income need from the portfolio of approximately $22,000. Natalie, who had 12 years of experience and held the Certified Financial Planner designation, conducted a thorough analysis. She noted that CD rates had peaked and the Federal Reserve was widely expected to begin cutting rates in 2024, which would reduce Dorothy's CD income upon maturity. Natalie prepared a written proposal recommending Dorothy move $510,000 (75% of the portfolio) into a diversified portfolio of investment-grade corporate bonds and U.S. Treasury bonds with laddered maturities from 2 to 10 years, yielding a weighted average of 5.1%. The remaining $170,000 would stay in a high-yield savings account as a liquidity reserve. Natalie's analysis showed the bond ladder would generate approximately $26,000 in annual interest income — exceeding Dorothy's $22,000 need — and that all bonds were rated A or higher. Natalie documented her reasoning in a detailed written memorandum, including the rate-cut risk to CDs, the credit quality of each bond, the laddered structure to manage reinvestment risk, and the liquidity reserve. The bonds were purchased at par or slight premiums. Natalie charged a one-time commission of 1.2% on the bond purchases ($6,120 total) with no ongoing advisory fee. Dorothy signed all disclosures and agreed to the plan. Over the next 10 months, interest rates declined by 75 basis points, and Dorothy's bond portfolio continued paying the locked-in coupons. However, Dorothy filed a complaint alleging that Natalie should not have moved her out of FDIC-insured CDs, that she was exposed to credit risk she didn't want, and that the $6,120 commission was excessive.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: No, this is likely not a violation. Natalie's recommendation was both suitable and consistent with the customer's best interest. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), the recommendation must have a reasonable basis, must be suitable for the specific customer, and must not involve excessive activity. Natalie satisfied reasonable-basis suitability by conducting a thorough analysis of rate-cut risk to Dorothy's existing CD income, selecting investment-grade (A-rated or higher) bonds to minimize credit risk, laddering maturities to manage reinvestment risk, and maintaining a substantial liquidity reserve. Customer-specific suitability was met because the bond ladder actually increased Dorothy's income from roughly $22,000 to $26,000 while preserving conservative positioning: investment-grade bonds with laddered maturities are a classic conservative income strategy. Under Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR 240.15l-1), the Care Obligation requires the advisor to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making recommendations, consider reasonably available alternatives, and ensure the recommendation is in the customer's best interest without placing the advisor's interest ahead of the customer's. Natalie documented her analysis, considered the alternative of staying in CDs (which carried reinvestment risk given the rate environment), and chose a well-matched conservative strategy. The 1.2% one-time commission on bond purchases is within industry norms and is not excessive under FINRA markup/markdown guidance (FINRA Rule 2121), which generally considers 5% as a benchmark for equity transactions and recognizes that bond commissions vary but 1-2% is standard for individual bond purchases. The Disclosure Obligation under Reg BI was met through Dorothy's signed disclosures. While Dorothy lost FDIC insurance, moving from CDs to A-rated bonds is a modest and well-documented step that addresses a real risk (rate cuts reducing future CD income) and is consistent with a conservative income objective. Dorothy's post-hoc complaint reflects an outcome-based grievance rather than a process-based deficiency.
why_adversarial: A general LLM is likely to side with the elderly, conservative customer and find a violation because: (1) the advisor moved a 72-year-old retiree out of FDIC-insured instruments, which sounds aggressive; (2) there is an emotional bias toward protecting elderly investors; (3) the client explicitly said she 'could not afford to lose principal' and bonds do carry credit and market risk. However, the recommendation was actually textbook-appropriate — investment-grade bond ladders are among the most common and conservative strategies for income-seeking retirees, the advisor's documentation was thorough, and the rate environment justified the move. The trap is that the advisor did extensive research and reached the RIGHT conclusion for this client, but a surface-level analysis focused on the loss of FDIC insurance and the client's stated conservatism would incorrectly flag this as unsuitable.
common_wrong_answer: Yes, violation. Dorothy explicitly stated she could not afford to lose principal and was very conservative. Moving 75% of a 72-year-old retiree's portfolio out of FDIC-insured CDs into bonds that carry credit risk and interest rate risk was inconsistent with her stated objectives. The advisor prioritized generating a commission over the client's clearly expressed preference for safety.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability — reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative components); Regulation Best Interest, 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Care Obligation, Disclosure Obligation, Conflict of Interest Obligation, Compliance Obligation); FINRA Rule 2121 (Fair Prices and Commissions); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor); FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (Additional Guidance on Suitability); SEC Regulation Best Interest Adopting Release, Exchange Act Release No. 86031 (June 5, 2019)

fact_pattern: Margaret Hollis, age 62, a retired school principal with $480,000 in total savings, purchased a variable annuity in January 2019 through her advisor, Derek Paulson, at Brightline Financial Group. The annuity had a 7-year surrender period, a 7% declining surrender charge, a guaranteed minimum income benefit rider with a 5% annual rollup, a mortality and expense charge of 1.35%, and total annual fees of approximately 3.10%. By December 2019, the annuity's account value had grown to $510,000. In February 2020, Derek left Brightline and moved to Keystone Wealth Advisors. Margaret followed Derek to Keystone. In March 2020, during the initial COVID market downturn, Derek recommended that Margaret surrender her Brightline annuity — paying a 6% surrender charge of $30,600 — and purchase a new variable annuity through Keystone. The new annuity had a 6-year surrender period, an 8% initial surrender charge, a guaranteed minimum income benefit rider with a 5.5% annual rollup, mortality and expense charges of 1.25%, and total annual fees of approximately 2.85%. Derek documented in his notes that the new annuity offered a superior rollup rate, slightly lower total fees, and a shorter surrender period. He also noted that the market downturn presented an opportunity because Margaret's guaranteed benefit base in the new annuity would start at the lower purchase amount, and the 5.5% rollup would compound on that base, potentially yielding a higher income stream at age 70 than staying in the old contract. Derek ran an illustration showing that if the market recovered modestly (6% average annual return), the new annuity's guaranteed income at age 70 would exceed the old annuity's guaranteed income by approximately $1,800 per year. However, Derek did not document or analyze what would happen if Margaret needed to access her funds before the new surrender period expired, did not compare the value of the existing rollup that had already been compounding for 13 months, and did not account for the fact that the old annuity's surrender charge would have declined to 4% within 24 months and 0% within 5 more years. Margaret's only other liquid assets were $95,000 in a bank savings account. Derek received a $14,200 commission on the new annuity sale. The recommendation was made on March 15, 2020.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, this is a violation. The critical temporal issue is that the recommendation was made on March 15, 2020, which falls after the June 30, 2020 compliance date for Regulation Best Interest — wait, actually the compliance date was June 30, 2020, so the March 2020 transaction falls under the prior FINRA suitability standard (FINRA Rule 2111) and FINRA Rule 2330 (Variable Annuity Transactions). Under FINRA Rule 2330(b), before recommending an exchange of a variable annuity, the advisor must consider: (1) whether the customer would incur a surrender charge or be subject to a new surrender period; (2) whether the customer would lose existing benefits; (3) whether the customer would benefit from product enhancements and improvements; and (4) whether the customer has had another exchange within the preceding 36 months. Derek's recommendation fails Rule 2330 analysis because: (a) Margaret paid $30,600 in surrender charges and restarted a new 8% surrender period, severely limiting her liquidity when she had only $95,000 in other liquid assets; (b) Derek forfeited 13 months of rollup compounding on the guaranteed benefit base; (c) his comparative analysis was incomplete — he only modeled a favorable scenario and ignored the liquidity risk, the lost rollup compounding, and the timeline for the old surrender charges to expire; (d) the marginal improvement of $1,800/year in projected income was speculative and contingent on market assumptions, while the $30,600 surrender cost was certain and immediate. Under FINRA Rule 2111's quantitative suitability and customer-specific suitability components, the switch was unsuitable because the concrete costs far outweighed the speculative marginal benefits. The advisor's documented rationale, while facially reasonable, omitted critical adverse factors, which is itself a violation of the reasonable-basis suitability obligation. Additionally, the commission of $14,200 raises concerns under FINRA Rule 2330's principal review requirements — the supervising principal at Keystone should have questioned whether the exchange served Margaret's interests or primarily generated compensation for Derek.
why_adversarial: A general LLM might get confused by the temporal aspect, potentially applying Regulation Best Interest (which took effect June 30, 2020) rather than the FINRA suitability rules and FINRA Rule 2330 that actually governed this March 2020 transaction. Additionally, the advisor's documentation appears thorough and facially reasonable — he ran illustrations, compared fees, and noted improvements — which could trick an LLM into finding compliance. The trap is that the analysis was selectively favorable, omitting critical adverse factors (lost rollup compounding, liquidity risk, declining surrender schedule on the old contract), which makes it a violation despite the appearance of diligence. An LLM might also overlook FINRA Rule 2330's specific annuity exchange requirements.
