Rowe Price Blue Chip Growth Fund into JPMorgan Large Cap Growth Fund (Class A shares, 5.25% front-end load), generating $6,562.50 in sales charges. David explained that JPMorgan's fund had outperformed T. Rowe Price over the trailing 12 months by 1.3%. In June 2020, after the COVID market recovery began, David switched the JPMorgan position back into T. Rowe Price Blue Chip Growth because 'market conditions had changed.' Margaret paid no load on this final switch but had held JPMorgan for only four months. David earned commissions on each Class A share purchase. His total commissions across all four transactions were approximately $12,400. Margaret's account value at the end of 2020 was $328,000, a net loss of $12,000 from her starting value despite the S&P 500 returning approximately 18% over the same period. David documented a rationale memo for each switch individually, and each memo contained a comparison of fund performance, expenses, and yield where applicable. Pinnacle Securities' compliance department reviewed and approved each switch at the time it was submitted.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: Yes, David Huang violated applicable standards on multiple levels. First, the switching pattern must be analyzed under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), which was the governing standard for the brokerage account through June 30, 2020, and Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), which took effect on June 30, 2020 and applied to the final June 2020 switch. Under FINRA Rule 2111, a broker must have a reasonable basis for believing that a recommended transaction is suitable for the customer. FINRA has long treated mutual fund switching as a red flag under Regulatory Notice 12-25 and earlier guidance (NTM 94-16), holding that switches between comparable funds that generate new sales charges without a corresponding meaningful benefit to the customer are presumptively unsuitable. The August 2019 switch into PIMCO Class A shares cost $3,562.50 in loads; the additional 1.4% yield differential would take approximately 2.7 years just to recoup the load — marginal for a 62-year-old moderate-risk investor when comparable no-load income funds existed. The February 2020 switch into JPMorgan Class A shares cost $6,562.50 based on a mere 1.3% trailing 12-month performance difference — an inadequate basis because short-term trailing performance is not a reasonable basis for switching, per FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25. That position was then liquidated only four months later, meaning the investor never had the opportunity to recoup the load. Under Reg BI's Care Obligation (17 CFR 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)), which governed the June 2020 switch, the advisor was required to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making the recommendation, considering costs. Switching back into the original fund after only four months demonstrates that the initial February 2020 switch lacked a reasonable basis. Viewed holistically, the pattern of switches generated $12,400 in commissions while the account underperformed the broad market by approximately $73,000 (the account lost $12,000 versus what an 18% return would have produced). The cost-to-equity ratio and turnover rate across these transactions, while perhaps not reaching the quantitative churning thresholds (typically 6x annual turnover under Goldberg factors), the switching activity constitutes qualitative churning and a series of unsuitable recommendations. The fact that compliance approved each switch individually does not cure the violation — compliance reviewed each in isolation without analyzing the cumulative pattern, which is itself a supervisory failure under FINRA Rule 3110.
why_adversarial: This is a temporal trap because the standard changed from FINRA Rule 2111 to Reg BI during the relevant period (June 30, 2020), meaning the last transaction must be analyzed under a different and arguably stricter standard. A general LLM might apply only one standard to all transactions. Additionally, the first switch (March 2019) was actually beneficial to the client — moving from a loaded fund to a no-load fund — which creates a false impression that David was acting in Margaret's interest throughout. Many models would either condemn all four switches or excuse them all, rather than parsing each individually. The compliance approval of each switch is a further trap, as models often treat compliance approval as exculpatory when it is not. Finally, the quantitative churning thresholds may not be met, trapping models into saying no churning occurred when the qualitative switching violation is clear.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely say this is a borderline case or not a violation, reasoning that (1) the advisor documented rationale memos for each switch, (2) compliance reviewed and approved each transaction, (3) the first switch was clearly beneficial to the client, and (4) the advisor provided performance or yield-based justifications for each recommendation. The model might also fail to recognize the temporal shift in applicable standards and apply only one framework uniformly.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) for transactions before June 30, 2020; SEC Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR 240.15l-1) Care Obligation and Cost Consideration for the June 2020 transaction; FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (Mutual Fund Switching); FINRA NTM 94-16 (Mutual Fund Sales Practice Obligations); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); Goldberg factors for churning analysis (excessive trading frequency, cost-to-equity ratio, control over account)

fact_pattern: Carlos Medina, age 41, is a software engineer earning $195,000 annually with a net worth of approximately $1.2 million, including a $650,000 home with $280,000 in remaining mortgage debt. He maintains a brokerage account at Redwood Financial with advisor Tanya Morrison. Carlos's account held $410,000 in diversified equity positions — approximately 60% large-cap U.S. equities, 25% international developed markets, and 15% in investment-grade corporate bond funds. His account documents listed his investment objective as 'growth,' risk tolerance as 'aggressive,' investment time horizon as '15+ years,' and annual income and liquid net worth were accurately recorded. In November 2023, Carlos contacted Tanya and said he wanted to use margin to purchase an additional $200,000 in a concentrated position — specifically shares of NVIDIA Corporation, which he believed would continue to appreciate due to AI demand. Carlos told Tanya he understood the risks of margin, had used margin at a prior brokerage firm five years earlier, and had read Redwood Financial's margin disclosure document, which he signed. Tanya explained to Carlos that a concentrated margin position in a single volatile technology stock could result in margin calls and amplified losses. She documented this conversation in her notes and in a follow-up email to Carlos. Carlos responded in writing: 'I understand the risks completely. I've been following NVIDIA for years and I'm confident in this trade. Please proceed.' Tanya executed the margin purchase of approximately $200,000 in NVIDIA shares. After the purchase, Carlos's account had total assets of approximately $610,000, with $200,000 in margin debt — a margin-to-equity ratio of approximately 32.8%. His total account was now approximately 33% concentrated in a single stock. Tanya did not recommend the trade — Carlos initiated it entirely, and Tanya's notes and emails clearly reflect that she counseled against the concentration risk. Redwood Financial's internal policy required a supervisor to approve any single-stock position exceeding 25% of account value in a margin account, but Tanya did not obtain supervisory approval before executing the trade because she understood the policy to apply only to advisor-recommended trades, not client-directed trades. The supervisor, when later asked, confirmed he was unaware of the trade until a routine monthly review.
question: Did the financial advisor violate the suitability or best interest of the customer requirements?
correct_answer: No, Tanya Morrison did not violate the suitability or best interest standards with respect to the recommendation analysis, but she DID violate her firm's internal supervisory procedures, which constitutes a separate regulatory violation. Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), the suitability obligation applies only to 'recommended' transactions. FINRA has clarified in Regulatory Notice 12-25 and the Supplementary Material to Rule 2111 (.03 and .07) that when a customer directs a transaction without any recommendation from the broker, the suitability rule is not triggered. Here, Carlos initiated the trade entirely on his own, Tanya did not recommend it, and Tanya actively counseled against the concentration risk — all documented in contemporaneous notes and email. Similarly, under Reg BI (17 CFR 240.15l-1), the Care Obligation applies only to recommendations. A broker who merely executes an unsolicited customer order is not making a recommendation and therefore does not trigger Reg BI's obligations. Carlos's profile — age 41, high income, aggressive risk tolerance, 15+ year time horizon, prior margin experience, and liquid net worth sufficient to absorb losses — further supports that even if this were analyzed as a recommendation, it would not be facially unsuitable given his documented profile, though the concentration would raise concerns. HOWEVER, Tanya violated Redwood Financial's internal concentration policy requiring supervisory pre-approval for single-stock positions exceeding 25% of account value in margin accounts. Her interpretation that the policy applied only to recommended trades is not supported by the policy's plain language as described. Failure to follow firm supervisory procedures constitutes a violation of FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision) and potentially FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade). The firm could also face liability under FINRA Rule 3110 for failing to have adequate systems to flag the concentration. So while there is no suitability or best interest violation, there IS a supervisory/procedural violation.
why_adversarial: This is a client direction trap combined with a subtle violation. Most general LLMs will either (a) say it's a clear violation because margin + concentration in a single volatile stock is unsuitable, failing to recognize that the suitability obligation does not apply to unsolicited customer-directed trades, or (b) say it's fully compliant because the client directed the trade and the advisor warned against it, missing the subtle but real violation of the firm's internal supervisory pre-approval requirement. The correct answer requires parsing the distinction between suitability obligations (not triggered) and internal supervisory compliance (violated). The NVIDIA detail is deliberately chosen because LLMs may have strong priors about concentrated tech stock positions being 'unsuitable' regardless of the recommendation analysis.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would most likely say this is a suitability violation, reasoning that allowing a client to take a concentrated 33% position in a single volatile technology stock on margin is inherently unsuitable regardless of who initiated the trade, and that the advisor had a duty to refuse the order. The model would likely conflate the advisor's duty to recommend suitable investments with a nonexistent duty to refuse unsolicited client-directed orders, and would probably miss the actual violation — the failure to obtain supervisory pre-approval under firm policy.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) and Supplementary Material .03 (meaning of 'recommendation') and .07 (customer-specific suitability); SEC Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR 240.15l-1) Care Obligation; FINRA Regulatory Notice 12-25 (FAQ on Suitability); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Rule 4210 (Margin Requirements); NASD Notice to Members 04-18 (Margin Disclosure)
